items.q: Capital of Egypt?
items.why: Founded by the Fatimids in AD 969, Cairo is now the largest city in the Arab world. The pyramids sit on its western edge at Giza.

items.q: What's generally counted as the first pyramid ever built?
items.why: Around 2670 BC Imhotep stacked six shrinking mastaba tombs at Saqqara for Djoser, creating the step pyramid that led to the smooth ones.

items.q: Nimsdai's full name?
items.why: Nirmal 'Nims' Purja, born in Nepal in 1983, became one of the most famous mountaineers in the world within a few years of his first 8,000er.

items.q: What's the 'forgetting curve'?
wrong: Memory fades at a steady rate
Memory fades only in old age
items.why: Hermann Ebbinghaus found in 1885 that most forgetting happens in the first hours and days, then levels off. Reviewing at the right moment resets the curve.

items.q: Who is Andrew Huberman?
items.why: He runs a neurobiology lab at Stanford School of Medicine and hosts the Huberman Lab podcast, one of the world's most popular science shows.

items.q: How many mountains are over 8,000 m?
items.why: All fourteen are in the Himalaya and Karakoram. Eight of them are in Nepal or on its border.

items.q: The 1956 workshop that coined the term 'artificial intelligence'?
items.why: John McCarthy organised the 1956 Dartmouth summer workshop and chose the name 'artificial intelligence' for its proposal.

items.q: Main language of Egypt?
items.why: Egyptian Arabic is the most widely understood dialect in the Arab world, thanks to decades of Egyptian films and TV.

items.q: Who's credited as architect of Djoser's Step Pyramid?
items.why: Imhotep was Djoser's vizier. Centuries later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of wisdom and medicine.

items.q: Nimsdai's 2019 mission to climb all 14 8,000ers was called…?
items.why: The name was a challenge to everyone who said it couldn't be done: all fourteen 8,000 m peaks in under seven months.

items.q: Who first measured the forgetting curve, by memorising nonsense syllables?
items.why: Ebbinghaus tested himself on thousands of syllables like 'DAX' and 'BUP' so meaning couldn't help, and charted how fast they faded.

items.q: Huberman's number-one daily habit?
items.why: Viewing outdoor light soon after waking sets the circadian clock: it times the morning cortisol pulse and the evening melatonin rise.

items.q: All the 8,000 m peaks are in which two ranges?
items.why: Both ranges were pushed up as the Indian plate rammed into Asia, a collision still lifting them a few millimetres a year.

items.q: Who coined 'artificial intelligence'?
items.why: McCarthy coined the term for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and later created the LISP programming language.

items.q: Egypt's currency?
items.why: Locals call it the 'geneih'. It's split into 100 piastres, and prices are often quoted in both.

items.q: Where is the Step Pyramid of Djoser?
items.why: Saqqara was the vast burial ground of the old capital Memphis, about 20 km south of modern Cairo.

items.q: How long did Project Possible take?
items.why: Nimsdai climbed all fourteen 8,000ers in 6 months and 6 days in 2019. The previous record was almost 8 years.

items.q: The spacing effect says you remember more when study is…?
items.why: The same total study time spread over days beats one long session, often by a wide margin. It's one of the most reliable findings in psychology.

items.q: How long does Huberman suggest for morning light on a clear day?
items.why: Outdoors even a cloudy sky gives far more light than indoors, so a clear morning needs only 5 to 10 minutes.

items.q: How many of the 14 are in Nepal or on its border?
items.why: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna all stand in Nepal or on its borders.

items.q: IBM's chess computer that beat Garry Kasparov in 1997?
items.why: Kasparov beat it in 1996, then lost the 1997 rematch 3.5 to 2.5: the first time a world champion lost a match to a computer.

items.q: The best-known local Egyptian lager, unrelated to the Belgian brand of the same name?
items.why: Egypt's Stella has been brewed in Cairo since 1897 and has nothing to do with Belgium's Stella Artois.

items.q: Roughly when was the Step Pyramid built?
items.why: Around 2670 BC, in the 3rd Dynasty: about a century before the Great Pyramid.

items.q: Which Netflix documentary follows Project Possible?
items.why: 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible (2021) follows Nimsdai Purja climbing all fourteen 8,000 m peaks in just over six months.

items.q: The 'testing effect' (retrieval practice) says the best way to learn is…?
items.why: Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it far more than reviewing it again. That's why Cerebrito asks you questions instead of showing facts.

items.q: How long does Huberman suggest for morning light on an overcast day?
items.why: Even through cloud, outdoor light is far brighter than indoors, but it takes longer to deliver the same signal to your body clock.

items.q: Height of Everest per the 2020 survey?
items.why: China and Nepal's joint 2020 survey measured 8,848.86 m, including the snow cap.

items.q: DeepMind's AI that beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016?
items.why: AlphaGo won 4 to 1. Its 'move 37' in game two looked like a mistake to experts, then turned out to be brilliant.

items.q: Egypt's cheap, beloved street dish of rice, lentils, macaroni, chickpeas and spicy tomato sauce?
items.why: A carb feast that mixes Italian pasta with an Indian-style rice and lentil dish, topped with crispy onions. It's cheap, filling and everywhere.

items.q: In the usual early sequence, which pyramid comes second, the one that later partly collapsed?
items.why: Meidum was probably finished by Sneferu. Its outer casing later slumped, leaving the tower-like core you see today.

items.q: Before climbing, Nimsdai served in the Gurkhas and which elite UK unit?
items.why: He joined the Gurkhas at 18 and in 2009 became the first Gurkha selected for the Special Boat Service, the Royal Navy's special forces.

items.q: Why does struggling to recall something help you learn it?
items.why: Psychologists call these 'desirable difficulties': retrieval that takes effort, but succeeds, leaves a stronger trace than easy recognition.

items.q: Why does window or sunglasses light work less well?
items.a: Glass and lenses filter much of the light's intensity
wrong: They block blue only at night
items.why: Window glass and sunglasses dim the light that reaches the cells setting your clock. Glasses or contacts for vision are fine.

items.q: Second-highest mountain in the world?
items.why: K2 (8,611 m) on the Pakistan–China border is far harder and deadlier to climb than Everest.

items.q: The 2017 Google paper that introduced the Transformer?
items.why: 'Attention Is All You Need' introduced the Transformer architecture, the T in GPT and the basis of models like Claude.

items.q: Which canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea?
items.why: Built under Ferdinand de Lesseps, the 193 km canal spares ships the long voyage around Africa. About an eighth of world trade passes through it.

items.q: Which pyramid changes angle halfway up because the builders feared it would collapse?
items.why: It starts at about 54 degrees, then eases to about 43 halfway up, probably after cracks appeared during construction.

items.q: What historic first did Nimsdai's Nepali team achieve in January 2021?
items.why: On 16 January 2021 ten Nepali climbers stepped onto K2's summit together, singing their national anthem. It was the last 8,000er unclimbed in winter.

items.q: Why is re-reading a weak way to study?
items.why: Text you've seen feels familiar, which creates an illusion of mastery. Testing yourself reveals what you can actually recall.

items.q: Which eye cells detect morning light to set your body clock?
items.a: Melanopsin ganglion cells in the retina
items.why: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells use melanopsin and report overall brightness to the brain's clock, not images.

items.q: Third-highest mountain?
items.why: At 8,586 m on the Nepal–India border, Kangchenjunga was thought to be the world's highest mountain until 1852.

items.q: When did ChatGPT launch?
items.why: Released on 30 November 2022, it reached about 100 million users in two months, then the fastest-growing app ever.

items.q: Which artefact let Champollion crack hieroglyphs in 1822?
items.why: French soldiers found it in 1799 near Rashid (Rosetta). Because the same text appears in a known language, Champollion could decode the hieroglyphs.

items.q: Which is considered the first true smooth-sided pyramid?
items.why: Built at the gentler 43-degree angle learned from the Bent Pyramid, it's named for its reddish limestone.

items.q: Who later beat Project Possible's time in 2023, finishing in 92 days?
items.why: Norwegian Kristin Harila and Tenjen Lama Sherpa climbed all fourteen in 92 days in 2023, roughly half Nimsdai's time.

items.q: Interleaving means…?
items.a: Mixing different topics in one session
items.why: Mixing problem types forces you to work out which approach fits each one. It feels harder but improves long-term learning and transfer.

items.q: Which brain region is the master circadian clock?
items.why: The suprachiasmatic nucleus sits just above where the optic nerves cross, so light can set it directly.

items.q: Height of Annapurna I?
items.why: 8,091 m, the tenth highest. Its south face is one of the biggest walls in the Himalaya.

items.q: The chips that power most AI training, made famous by Nvidia?
items.why: Graphics chips do thousands of small calculations in parallel, which happens to be exactly what neural networks need.

items.q: Where is the Rosetta Stone kept today?
items.why: When the French surrendered in Egypt in 1801, the stone passed to the British. It has been in the British Museum since 1802, and Egypt has asked for it back.

items.q: Which pharaoh built the Meidum, Bent and Red pyramids?
items.why: Sneferu, Khufu's father, built three pyramids as the Egyptians learned the right angle through trial and error.

items.q: Which cartel did Pablo Escobar lead?
items.why: At its height in the 1980s the Medellín Cartel is often said to have supplied around 80% of the cocaine reaching the US.

items.q: Which brain structure is vital for forming new long-term memories of facts and events?
items.why: The hippocampus binds new experiences into memories, then gradually hands them to the cortex for long-term storage.

items.q: What does early light do to cortisol?
items.why: A cortisol peak early in the day is healthy: it drives alertness. The same peak late in the day is linked to anxiety and poor sleep.

items.q: Annapurna I is ranked which number among the world's highest peaks?
items.why: Tenth of fourteen. It's not among the tallest, but for decades it was the most lethal.

items.q: Where does the word 'robot' come from?
items.why: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) introduced the word, from Czech 'robota', forced labour. His brother Josef suggested it.

items.q: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and which third script?
items.why: The decree, issued in 196 BC for Ptolemy V, was copied in three scripts. Scholars could read the Greek, which made it the key to the other two.

items.q: How was Sneferu related to Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid?
items.why: Sneferu's three pyramids were the learning curve. His son Khufu used the lessons to build the biggest of them all.

items.q: Escobar's notorious offer: 'plata o plomo' meant…?
items.a: Take a bribe or take a bullet
items.why: 'Silver or lead': accept a bribe or be killed. It's how he corrupted or terrorised officials.

items.q: Patient H.M. couldn't form new long-term memories after surgery removed parts of his…?
items.why: After 1953 surgery for epilepsy, Henry Molaison could hold a conversation but forgot it minutes later. He could still learn new motor skills, revealing separate memory systems.

items.q: Why does that early cortisol pulse help sleep later?
items.why: The morning pulse sets a clock: melatonin release follows roughly 12 to 16 hours later, so you get sleepy at a sensible time.

items.q: Which was the first 8,000 m peak ever climbed, in 1950?
items.why: A French team climbed it in June 1950, three years before Everest.

items.q: Who wrote the Three Laws of Robotics?
items.why: Asimov set them out in his 1942 story 'Runaround'. Many of his stories are about how the laws go wrong.

items.q: Which giant temples were cut apart and moved uphill in the 1960s to escape Lake Nasser?
items.why: In a UNESCO rescue from 1964 to 1968, engineers sawed Ramses II's temples into over a thousand blocks and rebuilt them 65 m higher.

items.q: Where are the Bent and Red pyramids?
items.why: Dahshur is about 40 km south of Cairo and far quieter than Giza, so you can see both pyramids almost alone.

items.q: What was the prison Escobar built for himself called?
items.why: He negotiated his 1991 surrender on condition he built the jail himself. It had a football pitch and a bar, and he walked out in 1992.

items.q: Roughly how many items can working memory hold at once?
items.why: Miller's famous 'seven, plus or minus two' has been revised down: modern estimates put it at about four chunks. That's why chunking helps.

items.q: What does Huberman say bright light between about 10pm and 4am does?
items.why: Bright light in the middle of the night shuts down melatonin and, he argues, can disturb dopamine and mood. Dim, low, warm light is the fix.

items.q: Who led and summited the first ascent of Annapurna in 1950?
items.why: Herzog and Lachenal summited without oxygen and lost fingers and toes to frostbite. His book 'Annapurna' became a classic.

items.q: The three 'godfathers of AI' who shared the 2018 Turing Award?
items.why: They kept faith in neural networks through decades when most of the field had given up on them.

items.q: The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, created which huge reservoir?
items.why: Lake Nasser stretches about 500 km into Sudan and is one of the largest man-made lakes on Earth. The dam ended the Nile's yearly floods.

items.q: Who built the Great Pyramid of Giza?
items.why: Khufu (Cheops in Greek) ruled in the 4th Dynasty. His pyramid used roughly 2.3 million blocks.

items.q: When was Escobar killed?
items.why: He was shot by Colombian police the day after his 44th birthday, ending a 16-month manhunt.

items.q: 'Chunking' helps memory by…?
items.why: 0412555918 is hard; 0412 555 918 is easy. Grouping turns many items into a few meaningful chunks that fit working memory.

items.q: Your body's core temperature naturally does what to start sleep?
items.why: A warm bath or shower before bed can help: it draws heat to the skin, then the body cools faster afterwards.

items.q: Annapurna I was long notorious for…?
items.a: The highest fatality rate of the 8,000ers
wrong: Having a road to the top
items.why: Avalanche-prone slopes gave it a historic death rate of around one climber for every three summits, though it has fallen recently.

items.q: Which AI pioneer shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics?
items.why: Hinton shared it with John Hopfield for foundational work that made modern machine learning with neural networks possible.

items.q: Roughly how far does the Nile run?
items.why: It flows north into the Mediterranean, and whether it or the Amazon is the world's longest river is still argued over.

items.q: Roughly when was the Great Pyramid finished?
items.why: Around 2560 BC, after about 20 years of work. Cleopatra lived closer in time to us than to its building.

items.q: Where was Escobar shot?
items.why: A police unit traced his radio call to a house in Los Olivos, Medellín. He died fleeing across the rooftops.

items.q: The 'memory palace' technique uses…?
items.why: The method of loci, used since ancient Greece: place vivid images at spots along a familiar route, then walk it in your mind to recall them.

items.q: The hormone of darkness that signals sleep?
items.why: Melatonin doesn't knock you out. It tells the body that night has begun, helping time when sleep comes.

items.q: Lowest of the fourteen 8,000ers?
items.why: Shishapangma, 8,027 m, is the only one of the fourteen entirely inside Tibet.

items.q: DeepMind's AI that predicts protein structures, winning a 2024 Chemistry Nobel?
items.why: Working out a protein's 3D shape used to take years in the lab. AlphaFold has predicted structures for about 200 million proteins.

items.q: Capital of Italy?
items.why: Rome became the capital of unified Italy in 1871. Legend dates its founding to 753 BC.

items.q: The Great Pyramid's original height?
items.why: It was about 146 m tall. Losing its smooth casing stones and capstone has cut it to about 139 m today.

items.q: Escobar's ranch that left Colombia with a growing population of…?
items.why: Escobar imported four hippos to Hacienda Nápoles. After his death they bred in the Magdalena River; there are now well over 100.

items.q: Memory champions mostly have…?
items.why: Brain scans show champions' brains aren't special. They use techniques like memory palaces, and ordinary people trained for six weeks improved dramatically.

items.q: What builds 'sleep pressure' in your brain the longer you're awake?
items.why: Adenosine builds up as you burn energy through the day. Sleep clears it, and caffeine temporarily blocks its receptors.

items.q: K2's brutal nickname?
items.why: After a deadly 1953 attempt, American climber George Bell said: 'It's a savage mountain that tries to kill you.'

items.q: DeepMind's co-founder who shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel?
items.why: A child chess prodigy and video game designer, Hassabis shared the prize with John Jumper and David Baker.

items.q: Italy's best-known mass-market beers?
items.why: Peroni has been brewed in Rome since 1846 and Moretti in Udine since 1859.

items.q: For about how long was the Great Pyramid the tallest human-made structure on Earth?
items.why: It held the record until Lincoln Cathedral's spire rose higher around 1311.

items.q: Which magazine listed Escobar among the world's billionaires?
items.why: Forbes listed him among the world's billionaires every year from 1987 to 1993.

items.q: The 'generation effect' says you remember better what you…?
items.why: Filling in a missing word or creating your own example makes it stick better than reading the complete version.

items.q: How does caffeine keep you alert?
items.why: Caffeine fits adenosine receptors without activating them, so the 'sleepy' signal can't land. The adenosine is still there when it wears off.

items.q: K2 sits on the border of which two countries?
items.why: It rises on the border of Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan and China's Xinjiang, deep in the Karakoram.

items.q: Boston Dynamics' famous humanoid robot?
items.why: Atlas became famous for parkour and backflip videos. The hydraulic version retired in 2024 for an all-electric one.

items.q: In what year was Italy unified as one kingdom?
items.why: Victor Emmanuel II became king of Italy in 1861 after campaigns led by Garibaldi and Cavour. Rome joined in 1870.

items.q: The three main Giza pyramids belong to Khufu, Khafre and…?
items.why: Menkaure was probably Khafre's son, so the three pyramids span three generations of one family.

items.q: The hit Netflix series about the hunt for Escobar?
items.why: Narcos, starring Wagner Moura as Escobar, followed the DEA agents on his trail from 2015.

items.q: Explaining an idea to someone else improves your own memory because…?
items.a: You have to rebuild it yourself
items.why: Teaching forces you to retrieve, organise and fill gaps, which is why the 'protégé effect' boosts the teacher's learning.

items.q: How long after waking does Huberman suggest delaying caffeine?
items.why: Waiting 90 to 120 minutes lets the body clear some adenosine first, which he says avoids the early-afternoon crash.

items.q: Who first summited Everest in 1953?
items.why: They reached the top on 29 May 1953 with a British expedition led by John Hunt. News broke on the Queen's coronation day.

items.q: Boston Dynamics' four-legged robot dog?
items.why: Spot has been sold commercially since 2020 and is used to inspect power plants, mines and construction sites.

items.q: When did Italy become a republic, voting out the monarchy?
items.why: Italians voted in a referendum on 2 June 1946, now celebrated as Festa della Repubblica.

items.q: Which is the smallest of the three main Giza pyramids?
items.why: At about 65 m it's less than half the height of the other two, though it was cased partly in costly red granite.

items.q: Which group of victims' families waged a violent campaign against Escobar?
items.why: 'Perseguidos por Pablo Escobar', people persecuted by Pablo. The group was backed by the rival Cali Cartel and paramilitaries.

items.q: When does the brain consolidate much of what you learned that day?
items.why: Overnight the hippocampus replays the day's patterns, moving them toward long-term storage in the cortex. Sleep after learning protects it.

items.q: Huberman's reasoning for delaying caffeine?
items.a: To avoid an afternoon crash as adenosine catches up
wrong: Caffeine is toxic in the morning
items.why: Caffeine only hides adenosine. Drinking it while adenosine is high means the full backlog lands when it wears off.

items.q: Where was Edmund Hillary from?
items.why: A beekeeper from Auckland, Hillary later spent decades building schools and hospitals in Nepal. He's on NZ's $5 note.

items.q: Tesla's humanoid robot?
items.why: Tesla announced it in 2021, memorably with a person dancing in a robot suit. It's meant to do repetitive factory work.

items.q: Roughly how many islands is Venice built on?
items.why: Venice spans about 118 small islands linked by more than 400 bridges over its canals.

items.q: Why does Khafre's pyramid look taller than Khufu's?
items.a: It sits on higher ground and keeps some casing at the top
wrong: It was rebuilt by the Romans
items.why: Khafre's pyramid stands on bedrock about 10 m higher, and still has original casing stones near its tip.

items.q: What did Escobar's group, 'Los Extraditables', fight above all?
items.why: Their slogan was 'Better a grave in Colombia than a jail cell in the United States'. Colombia banned extradition in 1991.

items.q: Pulling an all-nighter before an exam mainly hurts…?
items.why: Without sleep the hippocampus can't consolidate the day, and it's worse at taking in new memories the next day too.

items.q: Caffeine's half-life is roughly…?
items.why: About 5 hours, so half a 3pm coffee is still in your system at 8pm. That's why late caffeine wrecks deep sleep.

items.q: Who did the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen in 1978?
items.why: Doctors had warned the brain might not survive without bottled oxygen. In 1980 Messner climbed it again, alone.

items.q: Honda's pioneering walking humanoid robot from 2000?
items.why: ASIMO could walk, run and climb stairs. Honda ended its development in 2018.

items.q: What is Venice built on?
items.why: Millions of alder, oak and larch piles were driven into the lagoon mud. Starved of oxygen underwater, the wood petrified rather than rotted.

items.q: The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that…?
items.why: The other six, including the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria, were destroyed long ago.

items.q: Where was Alexander the Great born, in 356 BC?
items.why: Pella was the capital of Macedon, a kingdom the southern Greeks regarded as half-barbarian.

items.q: Napping after learning tends to…?
items.why: Even a short nap with some deep sleep can protect fresh memories. Long naps late in the day can hurt night-time sleep, though.

items.q: Roughly how long before bed does he suggest stopping caffeine?
items.why: With a half-life of about 5 hours, a quarter of the caffeine is still active after 10. It cuts deep sleep even if you fall asleep.

items.q: First person to climb all 14 of the 8,000ers (1986)?
items.why: Reinhold Messner finished the set in 1986, all without supplemental oxygen.

items.q: What does an LLM like Claude or ChatGPT fundamentally do?
items.a: Predicts the next token of text
items.why: It's trained to predict the next token, a word or word-piece. Doing that well across huge amounts of text produces surprisingly general abilities.

items.q: Venice's oldest bridge over the Grand Canal?
items.why: The stone bridge was finished in 1591, replacing wooden ones. For centuries it was the only way across the Grand Canal on foot.

items.q: What does the evidence say about who built the Giza pyramids?
items.why: Workers' villages, bakeries and tombs near the pyramids show paid, well-fed Egyptian crews, not slaves.

items.q: Who tutored the young Alexander?
items.why: Philip hired Aristotle in 343 BC. He gave Alexander a lifelong love of Homer and curiosity about science.

items.q: 'Neuroplasticity' means…?
wrong: The brain is made of plastic
items.why: Connections between neurons strengthen, weaken and reorganise with use throughout life. Training works because the brain adapts.

items.q: The 'physiological sigh' is…?
items.a: Two inhales through the nose then a long exhale
wrong: Holding your breath for a minute
items.why: A double inhale through the nose re-inflates collapsed air sacs, then a long exhale offloads carbon dioxide and slows the heart.

items.q: What's the 'death zone'?
items.why: Above roughly 8,000 m there's too little oxygen to acclimatise: the body deteriorates hour by hour, so climbers move up and down fast.

items.q: What's machine learning, in one line?
items.why: Instead of a programmer writing every rule, a model is shown many examples and adjusts itself to predict or decide from them.

items.q: Florence is called the birthplace of what?
items.why: In the 1400s Florence's wealth and rivalries drew Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli and later Leonardo and Michelangelo.

items.q: Which pharaoh is the Great Sphinx most often linked to?
items.why: It sits beside Khafre's causeway, and its face is generally thought to be his.

items.q: Alexander's father?
items.why: Philip II built the Macedonian army with its long-speared phalanx, then was assassinated in 336 BC.

items.q: 'Neurons that fire together…'
items.why: A summary of Donald Hebb's 1949 idea: when neurons repeatedly activate together, the connection between them strengthens.

items.q: What's the physiological sigh for?
items.a: The fastest real-time way to calm down
items.why: One to three sighs is the fastest known way to bring stress down in real time, because long exhales slow the heart.

items.q: Everest's dangerous shifting glacier near base camp?
items.why: The glacier moves about a metre a day, so 'icefall doctors' rebuild ladder routes through it all season.

items.q: Neural networks are loosely inspired by…?
items.why: Each artificial 'neuron' adds up weighted inputs and passes on a signal, a loose sketch of how brain cells fire.

items.q: Which banking family dominated Florence and backed Renaissance artists?
items.why: The Medici banked for the Pope, ran Florence for generations and produced four popes of their own.

items.q: The Great Sphinx has the body of which animal?
items.why: A lion's body with a king's head: royal power and strength combined, guarding the pyramids.

items.q: How old was Alexander when he became king?
items.why: He took the throne at 20 after his father's murder and crushed rebellions before invading Persia two years later.

items.q: Can adults grow new neurons?
items.why: Evidence suggests new neurons form in the adult hippocampus, though how much in humans is debated. Exercise appears to boost it.

items.q: What's NSDR?
items.a: Non-sleep deep rest, like yoga nidra
items.why: Non-sleep deep rest: lying still while guiding attention, as in yoga nidra. It's restorative without full sleep.

items.q: Everest's Nepali name?
items.why: Sagarmatha means roughly 'forehead of the sky', a name adopted in Nepal in the 1960s.

items.q: The 2012 image-recognition breakthrough that kicked off the deep learning boom?
items.why: AlexNet cut the ImageNet error rate from about 26% to 15% using GPUs. Hinton, Sutskever and Krizhevsky built it.

items.q: Who designed Florence Cathedral's great dome?
items.why: Built from 1420 to 1436 without a supporting wooden frame, it's still the largest brick dome ever built.

items.q: Roughly how long is the Great Sphinx?
items.why: About 73 m long and 20 m high, it's the largest monolithic statue in the world.

items.q: Alexander's famous horse?
items.why: Young Alexander tamed him by noticing the horse was afraid of its own shadow and turning him towards the sun.

items.q: London taxi drivers who learned 'the Knowledge' showed a larger…?
items.why: Eleanor Maguire's studies found the rear hippocampus grew as trainees memorised London's 25,000 streets, a famous case of adult plasticity.

items.q: Huberman's warning about 'stacking' dopamine?
items.a: Big peaks are followed by a drop below baseline
items.why: Stacking stimulants with everything you enjoy makes the baseline drop, so the activity alone starts to feel flat.

items.q: Everest's Tibetan name?
items.why: Chomolungma means 'goddess mother of the world'. The English name honours George Everest, a British surveyor.

items.q: What's an AI 'hallucination'?
items.why: A fluent, confident answer that's simply wrong. The model predicts plausible text, which isn't the same as checking facts.

items.q: Where is Michelangelo's David displayed?
items.why: Carved from 1501 to 1504, the 5 m statue moved indoors in 1873. The one in Piazza della Signoria is a copy.

items.q: The popular story that Napoleon's troops shot off the Sphinx's nose is…?
items.a: A myth, drawings show it missing earlier
wrong: True, but it was the British
Proven by a cannonball found inside
items.why: Drawings from the 1730s show it already noseless. A 15th-century writer blamed a Sufi zealot who damaged it in 1378.

items.q: Which Persian king did Alexander defeat at Issus and Gaugamela?
items.why: He beat Darius at Issus in 333 BC and Gaugamela in 331 BC. Darius was later killed by his own nobles.

items.q: Which habit has the strongest evidence for protecting the ageing brain?
items.why: Exercise raises BDNF, a growth factor for neurons, improves blood flow and is linked to a bigger hippocampus and lower dementia risk.

items.q: Roughly how much does cold water immersion raise dopamine in the study he cites?
items.why: In a 2000 study, an hour in 14 °C water raised dopamine about 250% above baseline, and it stayed elevated for hours.

items.q: Approximate altitude of Annapurna Base Camp?
items.why: Most trekkers reach it in about a week from Pokhara, climbing through rhododendron forest and bamboo.

items.q: Training vs inference: inference is when a model…?
items.a: Is used to answer, after training
items.why: Training is the expensive learning phase. Inference is every time the finished model answers a question.

items.q: Florence's medieval bridge lined with jewellers' shops?
items.why: Butchers once worked there. In 1593 the Medici replaced them with goldsmiths, and it was the only Florence bridge the Germans spared in 1944.

items.q: The Sphinx was carved mostly from…?
items.a: The living bedrock of the plateau
items.why: Builders quarried the limestone around an outcrop and shaped what remained, so the Sphinx is part of the plateau itself.

items.q: How did Alexander 'solve' the Gordian Knot?
items.why: Legend said whoever untied the knot at Gordium would rule Asia. A bold, lateral answer to an impossible puzzle.

items.q: BDNF, boosted by exercise, is often described as…?
items.why: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor supports neuron growth and new connections. Exercise is one of the most reliable ways to raise it.

items.q: Huberman's suggested weekly cold exposure total?
items.why: From Susanna Søberg's research: roughly 11 minutes of deliberate cold per week, split across 2 to 4 sessions.

items.q: The ring of peaks around Annapurna Base Camp is known as the…?
items.why: A high glacial basin ringed by Annapurna I, Hiunchuli and Machapuchare. You only enter through one narrow gorge.

items.q: Which company makes Claude?
items.why: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company founded in 2021.

items.q: How many villages make up the Cinque Terre?
items.why: Cinque Terre means 'five lands'. The villages are linked by cliff paths and a train through the hillside.

items.q: The Valley of the Kings sits across the Nile from which modern city?
items.why: Ancient Thebes straddled the Nile: temples for the living on the east bank, tombs for the dead in the western hills.

items.q: How far east did Alexander's army march before turning back?
items.why: At the Hyphasis (Beas) in 326 BC his exhausted army mutinied and refused to go further, so he turned back.

items.q: The 'Mozart effect' that music makes babies smarter is…?
items.why: A 1993 study found a brief boost in one spatial task in students. It never showed lasting intelligence gains, and later studies largely failed to replicate it.

items.q: Huberman's suggested weekly sauna total?
items.why: Roughly an hour a week, split over two or three sessions in a hot sauna, mirroring the Finnish studies he cites.

items.q: The sacred fishtail-shaped peak above the Annapurna trek, closed to climbing?
items.why: At 6,993 m it's sacred to Shiva. A 1957 team stopped just short of the top, and climbing has been banned since.

items.q: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by siblings…?
items.why: Both siblings came from OpenAI. Dario is CEO and Daniela is president.

items.q: The Cinque Terre villages: Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and…?
items.why: Riomaggiore is the southernmost of the five, its pastel houses stacked up a steep ravine.

items.q: The Valley of the Kings was the burial ground of which era's pharaohs?
items.why: New Kingdom pharaohs, roughly 1550 to 1070 BC, were buried here in over 60 hidden rock-cut tombs.

items.q: Did Alexander ever lose a battle he commanded?
items.why: In about 15 years of campaigning he never lost a battle he commanded, often against much larger armies.

items.q: Do we use only 10% of our brains?
items.why: Brain scans show activity across virtually all regions over a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems.

items.q: The 'Søberg principle' says to end on…?
items.why: Finishing cold forces your body to rewarm itself, which burns more energy and builds cold tolerance.

items.q: The lakeside gateway city to the Annapurna region?
items.why: Pokhara sits on Phewa Lake with the Annapurnas reflected in it, the base for most treks in the region.

items.q: OpenAI's CEO?
items.why: Altman has led OpenAI since 2019. In November 2023 the board fired him and he was reinstated within days.

items.q: Which region is the Cinque Terre in?
items.why: Liguria is the crescent of Italian Riviera around Genoa.

items.q: Why did New Kingdom pharaohs switch from pyramids to hidden rock tombs?
items.why: Pyramids were giant 'treasure here' signs and nearly all were robbed. Hidden tombs in a guarded valley were meant to be safer.

items.q: Where and at what age did Alexander die?
items.why: He died in 323 BC after a fever. Whether it was illness, drink or poison is still debated.

items.q: Brain training transfers best to…?
items.why: Training improves the trained skill and close relatives most. That's why Cerebrito trains many different skills plus real knowledge.

items.q: Focused work blocks Huberman recommends, matching natural cycles?
items.why: Attention seems to run in roughly 90-minute ultradian cycles, so longer deep-focus blocks hit diminishing returns.

items.q: Capital of Nepal?
items.why: The Kathmandu Valley holds seven UNESCO-listed monument zones, including Durbar Squares and the Boudhanath stupa.

items.q: Nvidia's leather-jacketed CEO?
items.why: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, reportedly over a meal at a Denny's. Its chips now power most AI training.

items.q: Which saint's relics lie in Bari's famous basilica?
items.why: Sailors from Bari took the relics from Myra (in modern Turkey) in 1087. St Nicholas is the original Santa Claus.

items.q: Who discovered Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922?
items.why: Peering in by candlelight in November 1922, Carter said he could see 'wonderful things'.

items.q: Which Homeric hero did Alexander idolise, honouring his tomb at Troy?
items.why: Plutarch says he slept with a copy of the Iliad, annotated by Aristotle, under his pillow.

items.q: Is multitasking efficient for the brain?
wrong: Yes, it runs tasks in parallel
items.why: For tasks that need attention, the brain switches back and forth, paying a 'switch cost' each time. Errors rise and speed falls.

items.q: The neurochemical cocktail Huberman links to alertness, released with cold?
items.why: Cold water can raise norepinephrine several-fold, which explains the alert, focused feeling that lasts after a plunge.

items.q: What's unique about Nepal's flag?
items.a: It's the only non-rectangular national flag
items.why: Two stacked pennants represent the Himalaya and the country's two great religions. The constitution explains how to draw it.

items.q: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 and bought by which company in 2014?
items.why: Google reportedly paid around £400 million in 2014. DeepMind went on to build AlphaGo and AlphaFold.

items.q: Bari is the capital of which region?
items.why: Puglia is the heel of Italy's boot, known for trulli houses, olive oil and orecchiette pasta.

items.q: Who funded Howard Carter's search for Tutankhamun?
items.why: The Earl of Carnarvon paid for years of fruitless digging and was about to give up when the tomb turned up.

items.q: Genghis Khan's birth name?
items.why: Born around 1162, Temüjin grew up an outcast after his father was poisoned, then united the Mongol tribes.

items.q: The 'Stroop effect' shows that…?
items.a: Reading is hard to switch off
wrong: Words are read right to left
items.why: Naming the ink colour of 'RED' printed in blue is slow because reading is automatic. Cerebrito's Ink game trains overriding it.

items.q: Roughly how long is one full sleep cycle?
items.why: About 90 minutes. Early cycles are rich in deep sleep, later ones in REM, which is why cutting the morning short costs REM.

items.q: Nepal's time zone offset from UTC?
items.why: Nepal keeps its own time, 15 minutes ahead of India, based on a meridian close to its own longitude.

items.q: The Taiwanese company that makes most of the world's most advanced chips?
items.why: Founded by Morris Chang in 1987, TSMC builds chips other companies design, including Apple's and Nvidia's.

items.q: Altamura's famous protected product?
items.why: Pane di Altamura, made from local durum wheat semolina, was the first bread in Europe to get protected (DOP) status.

items.q: Tutankhamun's tomb number in the Valley of the Kings?
items.why: KV means Kings' Valley. Tutankhamun's was the 62nd tomb found there.

items.q: In what year was Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan?
items.why: A great assembly, the kurultai, named him Genghis Khan in 1206, probably meaning 'universal' or 'fierce' ruler.

items.q: The 'cocktail party effect' is…?
items.a: Hearing your name in a noisy room
wrong: Getting tipsy faster in a crowd
items.why: Your brain filters out most background chatter but still monitors it, so your own name can break through.

items.q: In which sleep stage is most growth hormone released?
items.why: The biggest pulse comes in the first deep, slow-wave sleep of the night.

items.q: The trekker's staple meal of lentil soup and rice?
items.why: 'Dal bhat power, 24 hour' say the porters. On treks, refills are usually free, which makes it the best value meal on the trail.

items.q: Moore's law says the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every…?
items.why: Gordon Moore's 1965 prediction, revised in 1975 to roughly every two years, held for about half a century.

items.q: What famous prehistoric find was made in a cave near Altamura in 1993?
items.why: Altamura Man is a Neanderthal skeleton over 130,000 years old, so encrusted in limestone it has never been removed from the cave.

items.q: About how old was Tutankhamun when he became pharaoh?
items.why: A boy king of about nine, he reigned for around ten years, guided by powerful advisers.

items.q: The Mongol Empire became the largest…in history?
items.why: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire ever. The British Empire was bigger overall but spread across oceans.

items.q: Your 'default mode network' is most active when you…?
items.why: It's a set of brain regions active during daydreaming, remembering and imagining the future, and quieter during focused tasks.

items.q: What does alcohol before bed do to sleep?
items.why: Alcohol is sedating, which isn't the same as sleep. It fragments the night and suppresses REM, so you wake unrefreshed.

items.q: Nepal's famous steamed dumplings?
items.why: Momos came from Tibet with Newar traders and are now Nepal's favourite snack, steamed or fried with spicy chutney.

items.q: Who's often called the first computer programmer?
items.why: In 1843 she published what's seen as the first algorithm, for Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine.

items.q: Florence's famous art gallery with Botticelli's Birth of Venus?
items.why: The Uffizi was built as offices ('uffizi') for the Medici government, then became one of the world's first public galleries.

items.q: About how old was Tutankhamun when he died?
items.why: Scans show a broken leg and signs of malaria. How he died is still debated.

items.q: The Mongol relay-station postal system?
items.why: Riders changing horses at relay stations could carry messages hundreds of kilometres a day across the empire.

items.q: In the famous 'invisible gorilla' study, about how many viewers missed the gorilla?
items.why: Asked to count basketball passes, about half of viewers never noticed a person in a gorilla suit walking through. Attention is narrow.

items.q: Huberman's well-known sleep supplement 'stack'?
items.why: Magnesium threonate, apigenin (found in chamomile) and theanine. He stresses that light, timing and temperature come first.

items.q: Popular Nepali beers?
items.why: Most trekkers' summit-day beer is a Gorkha or an Everest, brewed in Nepal.

items.q: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
items.why: He proposed it at CERN in 1989 to share documents between scientists, and gave it away without a patent.

items.q: Which Pisa landmark leans because of soft ground?
items.why: It began tilting in the 1170s while still being built. Engineers stabilised it around 2001 by removing soil from under the high side.

items.q: Why is Tutankhamun so famous despite being a minor king?
items.a: His tomb was found almost intact
items.why: His small tomb was buried under debris from a later tomb, so robbers missed it. It was found almost intact in 1922.

items.q: What made Mongol armies so deadly?
items.why: Each warrior had several horses and a powerful composite bow, and the armies used feigned retreats to break enemy lines.

items.q: Huberman's stance on regular melatonin supplements?
wrong: The best sleep aid there is
items.why: Over-the-counter doses are often far higher than what the body makes, and he points to possible effects on other hormones.

items.q: Birthplace of the Buddha, in southern Nepal?
items.why: Siddhartha Gautama was born in Lumbini around the 5th or 6th century BC. A pillar by Emperor Ashoka marks the spot.

items.q: When did the first iPhone launch?
items.why: Steve Jobs unveiled it in January 2007 as 'an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator', all in one.

items.q: When did the Golden Gate Bridge open?
items.why: On opening in 1937 it had the longest suspension span in the world, a record it held until 1964.

items.q: Tutankhamun's innermost coffin is made of…?
items.why: The innermost coffin is solid gold and weighs about 110 kg.

items.q: When did Genghis Khan die?
items.why: He died in 1227 during a campaign against the Western Xia kingdom, possibly after a fall from his horse.

items.q: Bedroom temperature for good sleep should be…?
items.why: Core temperature needs to drop by 1 to 3 °C to fall and stay asleep. A cool room, around 18 °C, helps.

items.q: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a republic in…?
items.why: After a decade-long Maoist insurgency, Nepal ended 240 years of Shah kings and became a federal republic in 2008.

items.q: Alphabet's self-driving robotaxi company?
items.why: Waymo grew out of Google's 2009 self-driving project and runs paid rides with nobody in the driver's seat.

items.q: The Golden Gate Bridge's colour is officially called…?
items.why: It was meant to be a temporary primer. The architect kept it because it suits the setting and stands out in fog.

items.q: Tutankhamun's father is widely thought to be which 'heretic' pharaoh who worshipped one sun god?
items.why: DNA tests point to Akhenaten, who tried to replace Egypt's gods with the single sun disc, the Aten.

items.q: What's still unknown about Genghis Khan?
items.why: Legend says his funeral escort killed anyone who saw it, then horses trampled the grave flat. It has never been found.

items.q: What does Huberman say viewing the evening sun near sunset helps with?
items.a: Buffering the effects of artificial light later at night
items.why: He argues seeing the low evening sun makes your eyes less sensitive to artificial light later that night.

items.q: Was Nepal ever colonised?
items.why: It lost territory to Britain in 1816 but stayed independent, and its soldiers so impressed the British that they recruited them.

items.q: Quantum computers use units called…?
items.why: A qubit can hold a blend of 0 and 1 at once, which lets quantum computers attack certain problems in new ways.

items.q: The disaster that destroyed much of San Francisco in 1906?
items.a: An earthquake and the fires after it
items.why: The 1906 earthquake broke gas and water mains. Fires burned for days and destroyed about 80% of the city.

items.q: What was the 'curse of the pharaohs' story fuelled by?
items.a: Lord Carnarvon's death months after the tomb opened
items.why: Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in 1923 and the press did the rest. Carter lived until 1939.

items.q: Which grandson founded China's Yuan dynasty?
items.why: Kublai founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and ruled from Khanbaliq, today's Beijing.

items.q: Which sleep habit does Huberman call most important for a stable body clock?
items.why: Waking at the same time anchors the body clock, which then times your sleepiness the next night.

items.q: The famous Nepali soldiers in the British Army?
items.why: Gurkhas have served Britain since 1815. They carry the curved kukri knife and are famed for courage.

items.q: The robot widely used for minimally invasive surgery?
items.why: A surgeon sits at a console and steers tiny instruments through small incisions, with tremor filtered out.

items.q: San Francisco boomed after gold was found in California in…?
items.why: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848; the rush peaked in 1849, hence the 'Forty-Niners'.

items.q: Karnak Temple was mainly dedicated to which god?
items.why: Amun-Ra was the king of the gods in the New Kingdom, and his priests at Karnak became enormously wealthy.

items.q: Which Venetian traveller served at Kublai Khan's court?
items.why: Marco Polo spent about 17 years in China. His book amazed Europe with tales of paper money and vast cities.

items.q: The brain's waste-clearing system that ramps up during deep sleep?
items.why: During deep sleep, fluid flushes through brain tissue more freely, clearing waste including proteins linked to Alzheimer's.

items.q: The 7.8-magnitude quake that devastated Nepal struck in…?
items.why: The Gorkha earthquake of 25 April 2015 killed nearly 9,000 people and triggered a deadly avalanche at Everest base camp.

items.q: The NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2021 carrying a small helicopter?
items.why: Perseverance carried Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet in April 2021.

items.q: What's special about San Francisco's cable cars?
items.a: The last manually operated cable car system in the world
wrong: They're the oldest trams in Europe
items.why: Since 1873 a gripman has pulled a lever to clamp onto a cable running under the street. They're a National Historic Landmark.

items.q: What's Karnak famous for in size?
items.a: One of the largest religious complexes ever built
items.why: Covering about 80 hectares, it's one of the largest religious sites ever built.

items.q: Genghis Khan's empire made which trade route safe again?
items.why: Under the 'Pax Mongolica' merchants could cross Eurasia under Mongol protection.

items.q: Short sleep raises which hunger hormone?
items.why: Short sleep raises ghrelin (hunger) and lowers leptin (fullness), so you eat more, especially sugary food.

items.q: Nepal's currency?
items.why: The Nepalese rupee is pegged to the Indian rupee, at 1.6 to 1.

items.q: A model's 'parameters' are…?
items.why: Large models have billions of these numbers. Training nudges each one until the model's predictions improve.

items.q: San Francisco's famously crooked street?
items.why: The eight hairpin bends were built in 1922 because the hill was too steep for cars to climb straight up.

items.q: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall has how many giant columns?
items.why: 134 columns in 16 rows, the central ones about 21 m tall. Their carvings were once brightly painted.

items.q: Where was Napoleon born?
items.why: He was born in Ajaccio in 1769, just a year after France took Corsica from Genoa, and spoke French with an accent.

items.q: How much sleep do most adults need?
items.why: Sleep medicine bodies recommend 7 to 9 hours for adults. Regularly getting less raises the risk of many diseases.

items.q: Who are the Sherpas?
items.a: An ethnic group of the Everest region
items.why: Sherpa is an ethnic group, not a job title. They migrated from Tibet centuries ago and are famed for high-altitude mountaineering.

items.q: The tech region south of San Francisco?
items.why: Named in the 1970s after the silicon chip makers that clustered around Stanford and Palo Alto.

items.q: Karnak was linked to Luxor Temple by which avenue?
items.why: A road lined with hundreds of sphinxes ran about 2.7 km between the two temples. It reopened to the public in 2021.

items.q: When did Napoleon crown himself Emperor?
items.why: At Notre-Dame in 1804 he took the crown from Pope Pius VII and placed it on his own head.

items.q: Why does Huberman suggest using low lamps instead of overhead lights at night?
items.a: Light from above hits key retina cells
items.why: The light-sensing ganglion cells that signal 'daytime' sit mostly in the lower retina, so they look upward. Light from below barely triggers them.

items.q: Highest mountain in Peru?
items.why: Huascarán is the highest point in the tropics, and its summit is the furthest spot from Earth's centre after Chimborazo.

items.q: The San Francisco district of the 1967 'Summer of Love'?
items.why: In 1967 around 100,000 young people poured into Haight-Ashbury, the heart of the hippie movement.

items.q: Roughly how long did pharaohs keep adding to Karnak?
items.why: From the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemies, pharaohs added halls, pylons and obelisks for about two thousand years.

items.q: Napoleon's greatest victory, in 1805?
items.why: Called the Battle of the Three Emperors, it crushed Austria and Russia on 2 December 1805.

items.q: Roughly how bright is a sunny day compared with indoor lighting?
items.why: Sunlight is about 200 times brighter than a typical room, which is why indoor light barely registers with your body clock.

items.q: Huascarán's height?
items.why: Huascarán Sur is 6,768 m. Its slightly lower north summit was first climbed by Annie Peck in 1908.

items.q: San Francisco's historic beer brand, whose brewery closed in 2023?
items.why: Anchor made 'steam beer', a style unique to California. Its owner Sapporo closed the brewery in 2023.

items.q: Hatshepsut's mortuary temple is at which site?
items.why: Her terraced temple climbs into the cliffs at Deir el-Bahari, across the river from Luxor.

items.q: The 1812 campaign that wrecked Napoleon's Grande Armée?
items.why: Around 600,000 men marched into Russia. Burned cities, winter and disease destroyed all but a fraction of them.

items.q: The gland that releases melatonin?
items.why: The pineal gland releases melatonin when it's dark. Light at night shuts it off.

items.q: The Cordillera Blanca is the world's highest…?
items.why: Hundreds of glaciers sit within about 10 degrees of the equator here, though they're shrinking fast.

items.q: What language did the Incas speak?
items.why: Quechua, which speakers call 'runa simi', the people's language, was the empire's common tongue.

items.q: What was unusual about Hatshepsut?
items.a: She ruled as a full female pharaoh
items.why: She ruled for about 20 years around 1479 to 1458 BC, taking full kingly titles rather than acting as regent.

items.q: Napoleon's first exile island?
items.why: Exiled to Elba off Tuscany in 1814, he was even allowed to rule the little island. He escaped within a year.

items.q: Cortisol naturally peaks about how long after waking?
items.why: The cortisol awakening response peaks 30 to 45 minutes after waking and helps you feel alert.

items.q: Vallunaraju's height?
items.why: At 5,686 m it's popular as a first glaciated summit, climbed from a high camp above Huaraz.

items.q: Roughly how many people speak Quechua today?
items.why: Mostly in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador. It's the most widely spoken Indigenous language family in the Americas.

items.q: How was Hatshepsut often shown in statues?
items.why: Kingship was traditionally male, so official images showed her with the false beard and regalia of a pharaoh.

items.q: Napoleon's comeback after escaping Elba is called…?
items.why: He landed in France in March 1815 and marched on Paris as the army rallied to him, until Waterloo ended it.

items.q: One week of 5-hour nights lowered young men's testosterone by about…?
items.why: A 2011 study found a week of five-hour nights cut young men's daytime testosterone by 10 to 15%, like ageing 10 to 15 years.

items.q: Laguna 69 is famous for…?
items.a: Its startling turquoise water under glaciers
wrong: Being the deepest lake in Peru
items.why: Glaciers grind rock into fine 'flour' that stays suspended in the water and scatters light, turning it turquoise.

items.q: How do you say 'thank you' in Cusco Quechua?
items.why: Añay is common in Cusco. Learn one Quechua word before a trek and people's faces light up.

items.q: Hatshepsut's famous trade expedition went to which land?
items.why: Punt was probably on the Red Sea coast of the Horn of Africa. Her ships returned with myrrh trees, incense and ebony.

items.q: Who beat Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815?
items.why: Wellington's Anglo-allied army held on all day until Blücher's Prussians arrived on Napoleon's flank.

items.q: Box breathing uses which pattern?
items.a: Inhale, hold, exhale, hold, all equal counts
items.why: Inhale, hold, exhale, hold for equal counts, often four seconds each. It's a tool to stay calm and steady.

items.q: Which national park holds Laguna 69 and the Santa Cruz trek?
items.why: Huascarán National Park protects most of the Cordillera Blanca, including Peru's highest peak.

items.q: What does 'tupananchiskama' mean?
items.why: Quechua expresses parting as a promise to meet again, rather than a flat 'goodbye'.

items.q: Who's credited as the architect of Hatshepsut's temple?
items.why: Senenmut was her steward and trusted adviser, and possibly much more, if the gossip is to be believed.

items.q: Where did Napoleon die in 1821?
items.why: Saint Helena is a speck in the South Atlantic, nearly 2,000 km from Africa, chosen so he couldn't escape again.

items.q: Which elite military unit popularised box breathing?
items.why: Former SEAL Mark Divine popularised it as a way to stay calm and think clearly under pressure.

items.q: The 1970 Ancash earthquake triggered an avalanche off Huascarán that buried which town?
items.why: The 1970 quake sent an avalanche off Huascarán that buried Yungay in minutes. Only the cemetery hill survived.

items.q: Quechua famously lacks a simple word for…?
items.why: People say 'tupananchiskama', roughly 'until we meet again'.

items.q: Who later tried to erase Hatshepsut's images and name?
items.why: Her stepson and successor, probably late in his reign, to secure his own line's legitimacy.

items.q: Napoleon's lasting legal legacy?
items.why: The 1804 Civil Code set out equality before the law and property rights, and shaped legal systems around the world.

items.q: In the 2023 Stanford study Huberman co-led, 5 minutes a day of what improved mood most?
items.why: Cyclic sighing, with long exhales, beat box breathing, hyperventilation and mindfulness at improving mood and lowering breathing rate.

items.q: Which Cordillera Blanca peak was once voted 'world's most beautiful mountain'?
items.why: A 1966 vote in a German climbing magazine chose Alpamayo's near-perfect ice pyramid.

items.q: Which everyday English words come from Quechua?
items.why: 'Jerky' comes from 'ch'arki', dried meat. Quechua also gave English 'quinine' and 'guano'.

items.q: Alexander the Great took Egypt in 332 BC from which empire?
items.why: Egyptians resented Persian rule, so Alexander was welcomed in 332 BC as a liberator and crowned as pharaoh.

items.q: Was Napoleon unusually short?
items.a: No, about average height for his time
items.why: About 1.69 m, average for a Frenchman then. The myth came from confusing French and English inches and from British cartoons.

items.q: Cyclic hyperventilation, Wim Hof style, mainly does what?
items.why: Deliberate overbreathing raises adrenaline. A 2014 study found trained volunteers could dampen their inflammatory response.

items.q: Death Road's official name?
items.why: It runs about 64 km from La Cumbre pass down to Coroico in the Yungas cloud forest.

items.q: Besides Spanish and Quechua, Peru's other major Indigenous language?
items.why: Aymara is spoken by about two million people around Lake Titicaca in Peru and Bolivia.

items.q: Which desert oracle did Alexander visit, where he was hailed as son of Amun?
items.why: He trekked across the Western Desert to Siwa's oracle of Amun, which reportedly greeted him as the god's son.

items.q: What did Napoleon sell to the US in 1803?
items.why: The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States for about $15 million.

items.q: Which visual trick does Huberman say calms the stress response?
items.why: Widening your gaze to take in the whole scene (rather than focusing tightly) is linked to lower arousal in the brainstem.

items.q: Who built Death Road in the 1930s?
items.a: Paraguayan prisoners of war from the Chaco War
items.why: Paraguayan prisoners captured in the 1930s Chaco War were made to cut it into the mountainside.

items.q: Capital of Peru?
items.why: Pizarro founded Lima in 1535 as the 'City of Kings'. It sits in a coastal desert where it almost never rains.

items.q: Alexandria was founded by Alexander in roughly which year?
items.why: Laid out on a grid by the architect Dinocrates, it became the greatest city of the Greek world.

items.q: Which artefact did Napoleon's Egypt expedition discover?
items.why: His savants and soldiers found it in 1799, but the British took it as spoils when the French surrendered in 1801.

items.q: Stanford's Alia Crum found that viewing stress as what improves outcomes?
items.why: In her studies, seeing stress as something that sharpens you improved health and performance, even with the same stress.

items.q: Which organisation called it 'the world's most dangerous road' in 1995?
items.why: With sheer drops and no guardrails, the Inter-American Development Bank gave it the title in 1995. The name stuck.

items.q: Peru's best-known beers?
items.why: Cusqueña is the one you'll see at every trekking lodge, and Pilsen Callao is the classic everyday lager.

items.q: After Alexander died, which of his generals took Egypt and founded a dynasty?
items.why: Ptolemy even hijacked Alexander's body for Egypt. His dynasty ruled for nearly 300 years, ending with Cleopatra.

items.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BC?
items.why: Hannibal crossed with about 37 elephants, then crushed the Romans at Cannae in 216 BC, yet never took Rome.

items.q: Is short-term (acute) stress always harmful?
items.why: Brief stress can boost focus and immune readiness. It's chronic, unrelenting stress that does the damage.

items.q: Why do vehicles drive on the left on Death Road?
items.a: So downhill drivers can see their outer wheels at the cliff edge
wrong: It was built by the British
To keep trucks against the wall
items.why: Downhill drivers sit on the left in Bolivian cars, so driving on the left puts them by the cliff edge where they can watch their outer wheel.

items.q: Peru's national cocktail?
items.why: Pisco, lime, sugar syrup and egg white, finished with drops of bitters. Peru even has a national Pisco Sour Day.

items.q: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on which island?
items.why: The lighthouse was about 100 m tall. 'Pharos' still means lighthouse in several languages, like French 'phare'.

items.q: The Persian king who founded the Achaemenid Empire and freed the Jews of Babylon?
items.why: After taking Babylon in 539 BC, Cyrus let the exiled Jews return home and rebuild their temple.

items.q: Breathing through which does Huberman favour for most exercise and sleep?
items.why: The nose filters, warms and humidifies air and tends to slow your breathing, which calms the nervous system.

items.q: Roughly how far does Death Road drop?
items.why: You start in snow at about 4,650 m and finish in humid jungle around 1,200 m, all in one day of downhill riding.

items.q: Peru's bright yellow soft drink?
items.why: Launched in 1935 and flavoured with lemon verbena, it outsold Coca-Cola in Peru until Coke bought a stake in 1999.

items.q: What made the Library of Alexandria so significant?
items.a: It aimed to collect all the world's written knowledge
wrong: It was the first library ever
items.why: The Ptolemies tried to gather every book in the world, copying scrolls from ships in the harbour. It drew scholars like Eratosthenes.

items.q: Who was crowned Emperor of the Romans on Christmas Day, 800?
items.why: Pope Leo III crowned him in St Peter's, reviving the title of emperor in the West for the first time since 476.

items.q: Higher heart rate variability (HRV) generally signals…?
items.why: HRV is the beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm. Higher usually means a relaxed, adaptable nervous system.

items.q: Historically, about how many people died on Bolivia's Death Road each year?
items.why: Buses and trucks squeezing past each other on a single lane above huge drops made it notoriously deadly.

items.q: Purple-corn drink popular in Peru?
items.why: Purple corn is boiled with pineapple, cinnamon and cloves, then sweetened and served cold.

items.q: The Library tried to gather every book by…
items.a: Copying scrolls from ships in the harbour
items.why: Scrolls found on ships were copied. Often the library kept the originals and handed back the copies.

items.q: The Muslim sultan who retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187?
items.why: After the Battle of Hattin, Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187 and spared its people, unlike the Crusaders in 1099.

items.q: Where does Huberman say most of the actual rewiring from learning happens?
items.a: During sleep and deep rest afterwards
items.why: Practice flags which connections to change; the strengthening itself happens offline, during sleep and deep rest.

items.q: What changed for Bolivia's Death Road in 2006?
items.a: A new bypass road opened, leaving it mostly to cyclists
items.why: With traffic on the new road, the old one became Bolivia's most famous mountain-bike ride.

items.q: Raw fish 'cooked' in lime juice, Peru's national dish?
items.why: Lime acid firms the fish's proteins like gentle cooking. The leftover juice, 'leche de tigre', is drunk as a pick-me-up.

items.q: Which mathematician of Alexandria estimated Earth's circumference remarkably well?
items.why: Eratosthenes compared the angle of the Sun's shadow in Alexandria and Syene to estimate Earth's size remarkably well.

items.q: The Ottoman sultan who captured Constantinople in 1453?
items.why: Aged just 21, Mehmed breached Constantinople's walls with giant cannons, ending the Byzantine Empire.

items.q: What does Huberman say short pauses of about 10 seconds during learning allow?
items.a: Fast replay of what you learned
items.why: During brief rests the hippocampus replays the material at high speed, about ten times faster, which helps it stick.

items.q: Height of Huayna Potosí?
items.why: 6,088 m, and the trailhead is about an hour from La Paz, which is why it's called an accessible 6,000er.

items.q: Peruvian delicacy, roasted guinea pig?
items.why: Andean people have eaten guinea pig for millennia. Cusco Cathedral's Last Supper painting even shows one on the table.

items.q: Was the Library destroyed in one single fire?
items.why: Caesar's fire in 48 BC damaged it, but the Library mostly faded over centuries through lost funding and political purges.

items.q: Who unified China in 221 BC as its first emperor?
items.why: He standardised writing, coins, weights and even cart axle widths across China, and began linking its walls.

items.q: Huberman's quick tool to boost focus before work?
items.a: Fixing your eyes on one point for 30–60 seconds
items.why: Visual focus pulls mental focus along with it, so a minute of holding your gaze on one spot can sharpen attention.

items.q: Huayna Potosí is in which range?
items.why: The Cordillera Real is the snowy wall of peaks east of La Paz, including Illimani and Huayna Potosí.

items.q: Stir-fried beef dish showing Peru's Chinese 'chifa' influence?
items.why: Chinese immigrants from the 1800s brought the wok and soy sauce. It's served, very Peruvian-style, with both chips and rice.

items.q: Cleopatra VII belonged to which family?
items.a: The Ptolemies, of Macedonian Greek descent
items.why: The Ptolemies were Macedonian Greeks who often married their own siblings to keep power in the family.

items.q: Who led Britain through most of WWII?
items.why: He became prime minister in May 1940 as France fell, and refused to negotiate with Hitler.

items.q: The study Huberman cites found how much daily meditation improved attention and memory after 8 weeks?
items.why: Just 13 minutes a day for 8 weeks improved attention, memory and mood in non-meditators in a 2019 study.

items.q: Bolivia's highest mountain?
items.why: Sajama, an extinct volcano at 6,542 m, rises from a national park that holds some of the world's highest-altitude trees.

items.q: Huacachina, near Ica in Peru, is…?
items.why: A small lagoon near Ica ringed by huge sand dunes, famous for sandboarding and dune buggies.

items.q: Cleopatra was famous as the first of her dynasty to…?
items.why: Plutarch says she spoke many languages and was the first of her family to learn Egyptian, after nearly 300 years.

items.q: The Spartan king who held Thermopylae with 300 Spartans in 480 BC?
items.why: Leonidas held the narrow pass for three days until a local showed the Persians a mountain path around it.

items.q: What does Huberman say NSDR straight after learning can help with?
items.why: A short session of non-sleep deep rest after learning appears to help the brain consolidate what was just practised.

items.q: The mountain that dominates La Paz's skyline?
items.why: Illimani's triple summit, about 6,438 m, looms over the city and appears in its anthem and art.

items.q: Huacachina sits near which wine and pisco city?
items.why: Ica is the heart of Peru's grape and pisco country, a few minutes from the dunes of Huacachina.

items.q: How, according to Plutarch, did Cleopatra get to Julius Caesar past her brother's guards?
items.a: Smuggled in a bedding sack, popularly a rug
items.why: Plutarch describes a bedding sack. The rolled-up carpet is a later, more cinematic retelling.

items.q: The Mongol-Turkic conqueror Timur is better known in English as…?
items.why: 'Tamerlane' comes from the Persian 'Timur-i Lang', Timur the Lame, after injuries to his leg and arm.

items.q: Dopamine is mainly the molecule of…?
items.why: It drives wanting and pursuit more than pleasure itself, which is why anticipation can feel better than the reward.

items.q: Area of the Salar de Uyuni?
items.why: About 10,500 km², the remains of prehistoric lakes. In the wet season a thin film of water turns it into a giant mirror.

items.q: Giant ancient lines drawn in the desert of southern Peru?
items.why: Made roughly 500 BC to AD 500 by clearing reddish stones, figures like the hummingbird are best seen from the air.

items.q: Who carried Cleopatra in to meet Caesar?
items.why: Her loyal friend Apollodorus rowed her into Alexandria at dusk and carried her into the palace.

items.q: The 'Scourge of God' who led the Huns?
items.why: Attila's Huns terrorised both halves of the Roman Empire. He died in 453, reportedly on his wedding night.

items.q: To keep motivation high, Huberman suggests rewarding yourself…?
items.why: Intermittent rewards keep dopamine responsive. Reward every time and the baseline creeps up until nothing feels special.

items.q: What valuable metal lies under the Salar de Uyuni?
items.why: The brine beneath holds one of the world's biggest lithium resources, the metal in rechargeable batteries.

items.q: Peru's currency?
items.why: 'Sol' means sun, a nod to the Inca sun god. It replaced hyperinflation-hit currencies in 1991.

items.q: In what year did Cleopatra meet Caesar in Alexandria?
items.why: Cleopatra was about 21 and Caesar 52 when they met in 48 BC, while he was chasing Pompey's supporters.

items.q: The Zulu king whose army reshaped southern Africa in the 1820s?
items.why: Shaka introduced a short stabbing spear and the 'horns of the bull' formation, building the Zulu into a powerful kingdom.

items.q: Huberman's growth-mindset tip for hard tasks?
items.a: Learn to attach the reward to the effort itself
items.why: If you learn to feel rewarded by effort itself, the struggle fuels you instead of draining you.

items.q: Where's the best place in the world to see wild pumas?
items.why: Open steppe, plenty of guanacos and expert local trackers make Torres del Paine the best place to see wild pumas.

items.q: How many potato varieties is Peru said to have?
items.why: Potatoes were domesticated near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago, and Peru grows around 4,000 kinds.

items.q: Cleopatra was fighting a civil war against her brother. Who was he?
items.why: Ptolemy XIII lost to Caesar's forces and drowned in the Nile in 47 BC, leaving Cleopatra in charge.

items.q: The 14th-century Mali emperor often called the richest person in history?
items.why: On his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca he gave away so much gold that its price in Cairo stayed depressed for years.

items.q: Roughly what share of the body's serotonin is made in the gut?
items.why: Most serotonin is made by gut cells. It mostly works there and doesn't cross into the brain directly.

items.q: The puma, cougar and mountain lion are…?
items.why: One species, Puma concolor. It holds the record for the animal with the most names.

items.q: Lake shared by Peru and Bolivia, the highest navigable big lake?
items.why: At about 3,812 m, Titicaca is home to the Uros people's floating islands woven from totora reeds.

items.q: Cleopatra's son with Julius Caesar?
items.why: 'Little Caesar' was a threat to Octavian, who had him killed in 30 BC.

items.q: Where did Alan Turing work to break Enigma?
items.why: By 1945 nearly 10,000 people, most of them women, worked at the Buckinghamshire estate in total secrecy.

items.q: The 'bonding' hormone released by touch and closeness?
items.why: Oxytocin rises with touch, eye contact and closeness, and helps build trust and bonds between people.

items.q: Can pumas roar?
items.a: No, they purr, hiss and scream
items.why: Pumas lack the specialised voice box of lions and tigers, so they purr, hiss, whistle and scream instead.

items.q: Bolivia's constitutional capital?
items.why: Bolivia declared independence in Sucre in 1825. The Supreme Court still sits there.

items.q: After Caesar's murder, Cleopatra allied with and married which Roman?
items.why: Antony and Cleopatra had three children and ruled the East together, which Octavian painted as Rome betrayed.

items.q: The electromechanical machine Turing designed to crack Enigma settings?
items.why: Building on a Polish design, Turing and Gordon Welchman's Bombe ran through Enigma settings far faster than people could.

items.q: The 80-plus-year Harvard study found the strongest predictor of a happy, healthy life was…?
items.why: The Harvard Study of Adult Development found the quality of close relationships predicted health and happiness better than wealth or fame.

items.q: Largest cat in the Americas?
items.why: The jaguar is the third-largest cat in the world after the tiger and lion.

items.q: Which Bolivian city is the seat of government?
items.why: The president, congress and most ministries are in La Paz, so in practice it runs the country.

items.q: Which sea battle in 31 BC did Antony and Cleopatra lose to Octavian?
items.why: Octavian's admiral Agrippa won off western Greece. Antony and Cleopatra fled back to Egypt.

items.q: What was the Bombe called in the film The Imitation Game?
items.why: The film named it after Christopher Morcom, Turing's close school friend who died young. That's dramatic licence.

items.q: Which gratitude practice does Huberman say works most powerfully?
items.a: Receiving thanks or watching stories of people being helped
wrong: Writing a quick list of things
items.why: Studies he cites find receiving gratitude, or hearing a moving story of someone being helped, shifts mood more than listing things.

items.q: How does a jaguar often kill its prey?
items.a: A bite straight through the skull
items.why: Its bite is extraordinarily strong for its size, enough to crack skulls and turtle shells.

items.q: La Paz's altitude claim to fame?
items.why: At about 3,600 m, visitors often feel the altitude walking uphill from the airport, which is even higher.

items.q: How does tradition say Cleopatra died in 30 BC?
items.a: Bitten by an asp, a cobra
items.why: Plutarch reports an asp, the Egyptian cobra, but admits nobody knew for sure. Poison is just as likely.

items.q: Who played Turing in The Imitation Game (2014)?
items.why: Cumberbatch's performance earned him an Oscar nomination.

items.q: The 'runner's high' is now strongly linked to…?
items.why: Endocannabinoids, the body's own cannabis-like molecules, rise with sustained exercise and reduce anxiety and pain.

items.q: Jaguars, unusually for big cats, love…?
items.why: Jaguars are strong swimmers and hunt caimans and fish along rivers, especially in Brazil's Pantanal.

items.q: La Paz's cable car network?
items.why: Opened in 2014, it's the world's largest urban cable car network, linking La Paz with El Alto.

items.q: What happened to Egypt after Cleopatra's death?
items.why: Egypt became Augustus' personal province and Rome's breadbasket, shipping grain to feed the city.

items.q: Which country's codebreakers cracked early Enigma first and shared it with Britain?
items.why: Marian Rejewski and his Polish colleagues broke Enigma in 1932 and handed their work to Britain and France in July 1939.

items.q: Zone 2 cardio is a pace where you can…?
items.why: You can talk in full sentences but wouldn't want to sing. It trains the mitochondria that burn fat for fuel.

items.q: A puma's main prey in Patagonia?
items.why: Guanacos make up most of a Patagonian puma's diet, which keeps the two closely linked across the steppe.

items.q: The huge open-air market in El Alto?
items.why: Held on Thursdays and Sundays, it sprawls over kilometres of streets selling everything from car parts to puppies.

items.q: Why was Pompey the Great beheaded on arriving in Egypt in 48 BC?
items.why: Ptolemy XIII's advisers thought killing Caesar's rival would please him. Caesar reportedly wept when shown Pompey's head.

items.q: Enigma intelligence was code-named…?
items.why: 'Ultra' signalled a classification above Top Secret. Its existence wasn't made public until the 1970s.

items.q: Roughly how much Zone 2 per week does Huberman suggest?
items.why: Zone 2 is steady effort where you can still talk. A few hours a week builds the aerobic base that supports everything else.

items.q: Wild relative of the llama common in Patagonia?
items.why: Llamas were domesticated from wild guanacos thousands of years ago in the Andes.

items.q: What's sold at La Paz's Witches' Market?
items.a: Dried llama foetuses, potions and charms
items.why: The Mercado de las Brujas sells charms, herbs and offerings for Pachamama, mixing Aymara and Catholic tradition.

items.q: The legendary Egyptian 'Labyrinth' is at Hawara, beside the pyramid of which pharaoh?
items.why: Amenemhat III, of the Middle Kingdom's 12th Dynasty, built his pyramid and a huge temple complex at Hawara.

items.q: Historians estimate codebreaking shortened the war by about…?
items.why: Many historians estimate Ultra intelligence shortened the war in Europe by around two years, saving millions of lives.

items.q: What does VO2 max measure?
items.why: The most oxygen your body can take in and use during all-out exercise. It's one of the strongest predictors of longevity.

items.q: Wingspan of the Andean condor?
items.why: Up to about 3.3 m, among the widest of any land bird. Condors ride thermals for hours, hardly flapping.

items.q: Why are dried llama foetuses buried under new buildings?
items.a: As an offering to Pachamama for luck
items.why: Many people still bury an offering called a sullu under new buildings for the earth goddess's blessing.

items.q: Which Greek historian wrote that the Labyrinth surpassed even the pyramids?
items.why: Herodotus visited in the 5th century BC and claimed it had 3,000 rooms, half of them underground.

items.q: Turing's famous test for machine intelligence (1950)?
items.why: In a 1950 paper he proposed the 'imitation game': if you can't tell machine from human in conversation, call it thinking.

items.q: Why do longevity experts like Peter Attia focus on VO2 max?
items.a: It's one of the strongest predictors of lifespan
items.why: Large studies find people with low fitness have far higher death rates than fit people, more than smoking does.

items.q: Jaguars' spots have dots inside them. These rosettes are…?
items.a: Bigger and fewer than a leopard's
items.why: A jaguar's rosettes are larger with a dot inside, a quick way to tell it from a leopard.

items.q: The Indigenous women wrestlers of El Alto?
items.why: Women wrestle in traditional pollera skirts and bowler hats, a show that's also a statement of Indigenous pride.

items.q: The Hawara Labyrinth is in which region of Egypt?
items.why: The Faiyum is a fertile basin fed by a branch of the Nile, south-west of Cairo.

items.q: What happened to Turing in 1952?
wrong: He was made head of MI6
