items.why: Convicted of 'gross indecency', he accepted chemical castration instead of prison. He received a royal pardon in 2013.

items.q: The Norwegian 4x4 protocol for VO2 max is…?
items.why: Four intervals at about 90% of max heart rate, each followed by three minutes of easy recovery.

items.q: Roughly how big is the Amazon rainforest?
items.why: About 5.5 million km², larger than the whole European Union.

items.q: Bolivia's most common beers?
items.why: Paceña has been brewed in La Paz since 1886. Huari is the premium choice.

items.q: Why can't you see the Labyrinth like the pyramids?
items.a: It's buried and was largely quarried away
items.why: Flinders Petrie found its vast foundations in 1888. Much of the stone had been carted off for building in Roman times.

items.q: When did Turing receive a royal pardon?
items.why: The 2013 royal pardon was followed in 2017 by 'Turing's law', pardoning thousands of others convicted under the same laws.

items.q: Rep range typically used for building maximum strength?
items.why: Heavy sets of 3 to 5 reps train the nervous system to recruit more muscle fibres at once.

items.q: How many countries share the Amazon rainforest?
items.why: Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Bolivia, Guyana, Suriname and France, through French Guiana.

items.q: Bolivia's currency?
items.why: The boliviano replaced the peso boliviano in 1987. The sol is Peru's, the bolívar Venezuela's and the real Brazil's.

items.q: How was the Labyrinth's buried layout probed in 2008?
items.a: Ground-penetrating scans by the Mataha expedition
items.why: The Mataha expedition used ground-penetrating scans in 2008 and reported structures below the surface. It's never been excavated.

items.q: Whose face is on the Bank of England £50 note since 2021?
items.why: The note was issued on 23 June 2021, his birthday, with a quote: 'This is only a foretaste of what is to come.'

items.q: What actually drives muscle growth across a wide rep range (roughly 5–30)?
items.why: As long as sets end within a few reps of failure, light and heavy loads build similar muscle.

items.q: Which country holds about 60% of the Amazon?
items.why: Most of the forest, and most of the deforestation, is in Brazil.

items.q: Bolivia's first Indigenous president, elected 2005?
items.why: An Aymara former coca farmers' union leader, Morales governed from 2006 until 2019.

items.q: The Colosseum's official ancient name?
items.why: Named after the Flavian emperors who built it. 'Colosseum' probably came from a colossal statue of Nero next door.

items.q: What was Enigma's key weakness that codebreakers exploited?
items.a: A letter could never encrypt to itself
items.why: Because a letter could never encrypt to itself, a guessed word ('crib') could be slid along the message to rule out positions.

items.q: Roughly how many hard sets per muscle per week for growth?
items.why: Around 10+ challenging sets per muscle group per week is a common evidence-based target for hypertrophy.

items.q: Roughly what share of all fresh water flowing into the world's oceans comes from the Amazon River?
items.why: The Amazon carries more water than the next several largest rivers combined.

items.q: Bolivia is named after…?
items.why: Freshly independent in 1825, the country named itself after its liberator, Simón Bolívar.

items.q: Which emperor began the Colosseum around AD 70–72?
items.why: Vespasian funded it partly with treasure taken from Jerusalem in AD 70.

items.q: Where was Elon Musk born?
items.why: Born in Pretoria in 1971, Musk moved to Canada at 17 and then to the US for university.

items.q: Recommended rest between heavy strength sets?
items.why: Muscles need a few minutes to rebuild their fastest energy stores, so short rests sap heavy lifts.

items.q: Roughly how many trees are in the Amazon?
items.why: A 2013 survey estimated around 390 billion trees from about 16,000 species.

items.q: The famous revolutionary killed in Bolivia in 1967?
items.why: Che was captured and executed in October 1967 near La Higuera after a failed guerrilla campaign.

items.q: Which emperor opened the Colosseum in AD 80?
items.why: Vespasian died before it was finished; his son Titus opened it in AD 80.

items.q: Which payment company did Musk's X.com merge into?
items.why: X.com merged with Confinity in 2000 to form PayPal. eBay bought it in 2002 for $1.5 billion.

items.q: The principle of gradually increasing load, reps or difficulty?
items.why: Muscles adapt to what you ask of them. To keep adapting, the challenge has to keep rising.

items.q: About what share of the world's known species live in the Amazon?
items.why: About one in ten known species lives in the Amazon, and many more remain undescribed.

items.q: Which war cost Bolivia its coastline to Chile?
items.why: Fought 1879 to 1884 over nitrate-rich land. Bolivia still has a navy, which trains on Lake Titicaca.

items.q: How long did the Colosseum's opening games last?
items.why: According to Cassius Dio, about 9,000 animals were killed during the 100 days of opening games.

items.q: When was SpaceX founded?
items.why: He founded SpaceX in 2002 with money from the PayPal sale.

items.q: When do muscles actually grow?
wrong: Only while sleeping in the gym
items.why: Training is the signal; muscle protein is built over the following day or two, helped by food and sleep.

items.q: The Amazon's famous pink freshwater dolphin?
items.why: Botos get pinker with age, and local legend says they turn into charming men at night.

items.q: Despite being landlocked, Bolivia still keeps…?
items.a: A navy, training on Lake Titicaca
items.why: Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in 1884 but never let go of the claim. Every 23 March is its Day of the Sea.

items.q: About how many spectators could the Colosseum hold?
items.why: Estimates run from about 50,000 to 80,000, roughly a modern football stadium.

items.q: SpaceX's first rocket to reach orbit, on its 4th try in 2008?
items.why: After three failures, the fourth launch in September 2008 reached orbit when the company was nearly bankrupt.

items.q: What's DOMS?
items.why: Delayed-onset muscle soreness peaks a day or two after unfamiliar or eccentric work. It isn't a sign of a good workout.

items.q: Largest rodent in the world, found in the Amazon?
items.why: Capybaras weigh up to about 65 kg and are semi-aquatic, with webbed feet.

items.q: Bolivia's silver city whose Cerro Rico funded the Spanish Empire?
items.why: Silver from Cerro Rico made Potosí one of the world's largest cities by the 1600s. 'Vale un Potosí' means 'worth a fortune'.

items.q: The Colosseum was built on the site of which emperor's drained private lake?
items.why: Vespasian drained the lake of Nero's Golden House and gave the land back to the people as an arena.

items.q: When did SpaceX first land an orbital-class booster back on the ground?
items.why: In December 2015 a Falcon 9 first stage landed upright at Cape Canaveral, the start of rocket reuse.

items.q: The 'eccentric' phase of a lift is when the muscle…?
items.why: Like lowering the bar in a curl. Eccentrics cause more soreness but are powerful for strength and tendon health.

items.q: The world's heaviest snake, found in Amazon rivers?
items.why: Female green anacondas are much bigger than males and can outweigh a grown man.

items.q: San Pedro prison in La Paz is famous because…?
items.a: Inmates buy or rent their cells and families live inside
items.why: There are few guards inside. Inmates run the place, pay for their cells, and some have families living with them.

items.q: What was the hypogeum?
items.why: A two-level warren of tunnels, cages and lifts under the floor, used to send animals and scenery up through trapdoors.

items.q: SpaceX's first crewed flight to the ISS, Demo-2, launched in…?
items.why: Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley flew in May 2020, the first crew launched from the US since the Space Shuttle retired.

items.q: Which is a compound lift?
items.why: A compound lift moves several joints at once, like squats, deadlifts and presses, training more muscle per set.

items.q: The giant Amazon fish that breathes air?
items.why: Arapaima can grow to about 3 m. They must surface every few minutes to gulp air.

items.q: Which book tells the story of a British inmate in San Pedro?
items.why: Marching Powder, published in 2003, became a backpacker classic.

items.q: What was the velarium?
items.a: A huge retractable awning for shade
items.why: Sailors from the Roman fleet rigged the vast canvas awning to shade spectators.

items.q: What did SpaceX first do with Starship's booster in October 2024?
items.why: The Super Heavy booster was caught mid-air by the launch tower's 'chopstick' arms on 13 October 2024.

items.q: Grip strength is linked in research to…?
items.why: Large studies find stronger grip predicts lower all-cause mortality. It's a proxy for overall strength.

items.q: Amazon tree-dwellers that move so slowly algae grows on their fur?
items.why: Moving so slowly helps them hide from eagles and jaguars, and the green algae adds camouflage.

items.q: Who wrote Marching Powder?
items.why: Rusty Young, a young Australian law graduate, lived inside the prison for months to write it.

items.q: How did animals and scenery appear suddenly in the arena?
items.a: Lifts and trapdoors from the hypogeum
items.why: Dozens of lifts worked by winches raised animals and scenery through trapdoors in the floor.

items.q: SpaceX's satellite internet service?
items.why: Starlink uses thousands of satellites in low orbit to beam internet almost anywhere.

items.q: Huberman suggests keeping workouts to roughly how long after warm-up?
items.why: He argues that past about an hour of hard training, returns fall as fatigue and stress hormones climb.

items.q: What do the Amazon's tiny, bright 'poison dart' frogs warn predators with?
items.why: Bright colours advertise poison, a strategy called aposematism. Captive-bred frogs aren't toxic because they lack their wild diet.

items.q: The British drug trafficker at the heart of Marching Powder?
items.why: Thomas McFadden was arrested at La Paz airport with cocaine and spent years in San Pedro.

items.q: Where does the word 'arena' come from?
items.a: Latin for sand, spread to soak up blood
items.why: Latin 'harena' meant sand. It soaked up blood and gave fighters grip.

items.q: SpaceX's long-term goal?
items.why: Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with the aim of making humanity multiplanetary, starting with a city on Mars.

items.q: In Huberman's weekly fitness protocol, Sunday is usually…?
items.why: He uses Sunday for a long, steady Zone 2 session such as a 60 to 75 minute run, hike or ruck.

items.q: Where the Rio Negro and Solimões meet without mixing for kilometres?
items.why: The Meeting of the Waters: dark, warm Rio Negro and pale, cooler Solimões run side by side for about 6 km.

items.q: What did McFadden famously run inside the prison?
items.why: He bribed guards to let backpackers in for tours, which even made it into guidebooks.

items.q: What was a typical order of a day at the Colosseum?
items.why: Animal hunts filled the morning, executions the midday, and the star gladiator bouts came in the afternoon.

items.q: Did Musk found Tesla?
items.a: No, but he's called a co-founder
items.why: Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning founded Tesla in 2003. Musk led the 2004 funding round and a 2009 settlement lets him use 'co-founder'.

items.q: Who's the exercise scientist Huberman often brings on for training advice?
items.why: Andy Galpin is a professor of kinesiology who studies how muscle adapts to training.

items.q: Bolivia's gateway town to the Amazon and Madidi?
items.why: Rurrenabaque sits on the Beni River, the jumping-off point for Madidi's jungle and the pampas wetlands.

items.q: Capital of Argentina?
items.why: People from Buenos Aires are 'porteños', people of the port, a nod to its history as a trading hub.

items.q: What were 'venationes'?
items.why: Hunts with exotic beasts usually filled the morning programme.

items.q: Tesla's first car?
items.why: The Roadster was built on a Lotus chassis. Musk's own was later launched into space on a Falcon Heavy.

items.q: Huberman says avoid cold plunges for several hours after hypertrophy training because…?
items.a: Cold may blunt muscle growth adaptations
items.why: Cold dampens the inflammation and signalling that drive muscle growth, so separate the two by several hours.

items.q: Argentina's most common beer?
items.why: Brewed since 1890 in the town of Quilmes, its blue and white label matches the national team.

items.q: Which exotic animals were brought to the arena?
items.a: Lions, leopards, bears, elephants and more
items.why: Animals were shipped in from across the empire, draining parts of North Africa of big wildlife.

items.q: Musk's brain-computer interface company?
items.why: Neuralink implanted its first device in a human in 2024, letting a paralysed man move a cursor by thought.

items.q: Is lactate just a waste product that causes soreness?
items.a: No, it's also a fuel your body uses
items.why: Lactate is a fuel the heart and muscles burn and a signalling molecule. It isn't what makes you sore.

items.q: Argentina's cult drink of Fernet mixed with…?
items.why: Argentina drinks more Fernet than anywhere, and Fernet con Coca is practically Córdoba's official drink.

items.q: Who's often blamed for the Colosseum's missing outer ring?
items.why: A big earthquake in 1349 brought down the south side, and the fallen stone was quarried for centuries, including for St Peter's.

items.q: Musk's AI company that makes Grok?
items.why: Musk founded xAI in 2023. Its chatbot Grok is built into X.

items.q: Zone 2 training especially builds more…?
items.why: Steady aerobic work makes muscles build more and better mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

items.q: The herbal drink sipped from a gourd through a metal straw?
items.why: Mate is shared: one person, the cebador, refills the gourd and passes it round the group.

items.q: How was the crowd seated?
items.why: Senators sat at the front and women and the poor right at the top, as Augustus' laws required.

items.q: Which AI lab did Musk co-found in 2015 before leaving its board in 2018?
items.why: He was an early co-founder and funder, left the board in 2018, and later sued the company.

items.q: Peter Attia's book about living longer and better?
items.why: Published in 2023, Outlive argues for training strength, cardio and stability early to protect the last decade of life.

items.q: The metal straw used for mate?
items.why: The bombilla has a filter at the bottom so you sip the infusion without the leaves.

items.q: What was a naumachia?
items.why: Early on the arena may have been flooded for mock sea battles, before the underground hypogeum was built.

items.q: What did Musk buy for about $44 billion in 2022 and rename X?
items.why: The deal closed in October 2022. The bird logo was replaced by an X the following year.

items.q: Peter Attia's idea of training now for the 10 physical tasks you want to do in your final decade?
items.why: Pick the ten things you want to do at 90, like lifting a grandchild or climbing stairs, then train for them now.

items.q: Argentina's famous grape, especially from Mendoza?
items.why: Malbec came from south-west France and thrived in Mendoza's high, sunny vineyards.

items.q: Who were most gladiators?
items.why: Mostly slaves, prisoners of war and condemned criminals, though some free men signed up for fame and money.

items.q: Musk's tunnelling company?
items.why: The name is a pun. Its best-known project is a tunnel loop under the Las Vegas Convention Center.

items.q: The calories you burn through non-exercise movement like walking and fidgeting?
items.why: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis can differ between people by several hundred calories a day.

items.q: Highest mountain in the Americas, near Mendoza?
items.why: At 6,961 m it's the highest mountain outside Asia and one of the Seven Summits.

items.q: Did free men ever choose to become gladiators?
items.why: Volunteers (auctorati) swore an oath giving up their rights, chasing prize money and celebrity.

items.q: Basic recommended daily protein for the average adult?
items.a: About 0.8 g per kg of bodyweight
items.why: 0.8 g per kg is the minimum to avoid deficiency, not the amount that best supports muscle as you age.

items.q: Aconcagua's height?
items.why: Its normal route isn't technical, but altitude, cold and fierce winds turn back many climbers.

items.q: A gladiator armed with a net and trident was a…?
items.why: The retiarius fought nearly unarmoured, relying on speed, reach and the net. He was often seen as the lowest rank.

items.q: A common protein target Huberman and Galpin give for people training hard?
items.a: About 1 g per pound of bodyweight
wrong: Double the bodyweight in grams per meal
items.why: 1 g per pound is about 2.2 g per kg. Research suggests most of the benefit comes by about 1.6 g per kg.

items.q: Bariloche is famous for…?
items.why: Bariloche on Lake Nahuel Huapi looks like a slice of the Alps, chalets and chocolate shops included.

items.q: The heavily armed gladiator usually matched against the net-man?
items.why: The secutor, 'chaser', wore a smooth round helmet so the net couldn't snag it.

items.q: Which amino acid is key for switching on muscle protein synthesis?
items.why: Leucine acts as a trigger for muscle building, which is why protein quality matters, not just quantity.

items.q: The world-famous glacier near El Calafate?
items.why: Unlike most glaciers it isn't shrinking much. Every few years its ice dam ruptures in a spectacular collapse.

items.q: Gladiator with a big rectangular shield and a fish-crested helmet?
items.why: The murmillo's crest was shaped like a fish, the 'mormylos', a natural foe for the net-man.

items.q: Typical daily dose of creatine monohydrate?
items.why: About 5 g a day saturates muscle stores within a few weeks. No loading phase is needed.

items.q: Argentina's self-styled 'trekking capital', beneath Fitz Roy?
items.why: El Chaltén was founded in 1985, partly to secure Argentina's claim to the area. It's built for hikers.

items.q: Gladiator with a small shield and a curved short sword?
items.why: The thraex fought with a curved sica, a weapon associated with Thracian warriors.

items.q: Besides muscle, creatine is being studied for benefits to…?
items.why: The brain also runs on creatine-based energy, and benefits seem clearest when sleep-deprived or on a meat-free diet.

items.q: The 'southernmost city in the world'?
items.why: Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, is the main departure port for Antarctic cruises.

items.q: What did a gladiator receive to mark his freedom?
items.why: The wooden rudis marked a gladiator's release from the arena, sometimes awarded on the spot by the crowd.

items.q: The 'Galpin equation' for drinking during exercise?
items.a: Bodyweight in pounds ÷ 30 = ounces every 15 minutes
items.why: So someone weighing 180 lb drinks about 6 oz, roughly 180 ml, every 15 minutes of exercise.

items.q: Who's the famous former First Lady, 'Evita'?
items.why: Eva Perón championed workers and women's suffrage and died of cancer in 1952, aged just 33.

items.q: Who decided whether a beaten gladiator lived?
items.a: The host, swayed by the crowd
items.why: The editor (often the emperor) made the call, usually following the crowd's mood. Good fighters were valuable, so many were spared.

items.q: The three main electrolytes Huberman talks about?
items.why: Nerves fire using sodium and potassium, so being low can cause fatigue, cramps and brain fog.

items.q: Argentina's 1982 war with Britain was over which islands?
items.why: Argentina invaded in April 1982; Britain retook the islands after a 74-day war. Argentina still claims them.

items.q: The idea that 'thumbs down' meant death is…?
items.a: Uncertain, the real gesture is debated
items.why: Romans did use a thumb gesture ('pollice verso'), but which way meant death is unknown. The thumbs-down idea comes from a 19th-century painting.

items.q: Caffeine dose shown to boost exercise performance?
items.why: The sports-science consensus range is 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight, about an hour before. Lower doses around 2 mg/kg can help too.

items.q: How many men's World Cups has Argentina won?
items.why: 1978 at home, 1986 with Maradona, and 2022 in Qatar with Messi.

items.q: Did most gladiator fights end in death?
items.a: No, many ended with the loser spared
items.why: Gladiators were expensive to train, so many bouts ended with the loser spared. Estimates suggest maybe one in five fights was fatal.

items.q: In the Stanford fermented-food study, eating more fermented food led to…?
items.why: In the 2021 study, people eating fermented foods daily for ten weeks gained microbe diversity and showed lower inflammatory markers.

items.q: Buenos Aires's colourful street in La Boca?
items.why: The houses were painted with leftover ship paint. The street is named after a famous tango.

items.q: Which gladiator led a huge slave revolt in 73–71 BC?
items.why: Spartacus's army grew to tens of thousands. After it was defeated, 6,000 rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.

items.q: Roughly how many servings of fermented food a day does Huberman suggest?
items.why: Based on the Stanford study: small daily servings of things like yoghurt, kefir, kimchi or sauerkraut.

items.q: Famous Buenos Aires cemetery where Evita is buried?
items.why: Recoleta Cemetery is a city of marble mausoleums. Evita lies in her family's tomb, the Duarte vault.

items.q: Which emperor fought in the arena himself, shocking Rome?
items.why: Commodus fought staged bouts as a gladiator, a scandal for an emperor. The film Gladiator is loosely based on him.

items.q: Which omega-3 does Huberman highlight for mood, at about 1 g or more a day?
items.why: Trials suggest a gram or more of EPA a day can lift mood, sometimes as an add-on to other treatment.

items.q: The giant waterfalls on the Argentina–Brazil border?
items.why: About 275 falls stretch nearly 3 km. Eleanor Roosevelt is said to have exclaimed 'Poor Niagara!'

items.q: What diet did gladiators reportedly eat, earning the nickname 'barley men'?
items.why: Bones from a gladiator cemetery at Ephesus show a mostly plant-based diet, and possibly a plant-ash drink for calcium.

items.q: Vitamin D is mainly made by the body from…?
items.why: UVB on the skin makes vitamin D. Far from the equator in winter there's too little, so supplements are common.

items.q: Argentine slang for 'cool' or 'great'?
items.why: Copado means cool or great. You'll hear it constantly alongside 'genial' and 're bueno'.

items.q: Gladiators trained at schools called…?
items.why: The biggest, the Ludus Magnus, was connected to the Colosseum by a tunnel.

items.q: The Salk researcher behind time-restricted eating that Huberman often features?
items.why: Satchin Panda's research suggests eating within a consistent window of 8 to 12 hours helps metabolic health.

items.q: Who's the Argentine-born revolutionary famed in Cuba?
items.why: Born in Rosario in 1928, he was nicknamed for the Argentine habit of saying 'che', roughly 'hey, mate'.

items.q: What did gladiators supposedly say before fighting, according to Suetonius?
items.a: 'Those who are about to die salute you'
items.why: 'Ave, imperator, morituri te salutant.' Suetonius records it once, at a mock sea battle under Claudius, so it may not have been routine.

items.q: A short walk after a meal does what to blood sugar?
items.why: Working muscles pull glucose from the blood, so even 10 minutes of walking flattens the post-meal rise.

items.q: The hero of Argentine independence who crossed the Andes in 1817?
items.why: With about 5,000 men he crossed the Andes in 1817 to free Chile, then sailed north to liberate Peru.

items.q: What powered Roman aqueducts?
items.a: Gravity, with a gentle steady slope
items.why: Gravity alone. Engineers kept a slight, steady downhill gradient over many kilometres, sometimes as little as 1 in 4,800.

items.q: What toxic compound does the body first turn alcohol into?
items.why: Acetaldehyde causes much of a hangover. People with a slower enzyme to clear it get the 'Asian flush'.

items.q: Argentina's famous caramel spread?
items.why: Milk and sugar simmered for hours until the sugars caramelise. Argentines put it on everything.

items.q: Rome's first aqueduct, built in 312 BC?
items.why: Built by Appius Claudius, who also built the Appian Way, it ran almost entirely underground.

items.q: Huberman's conclusion after his alcohol episode?
items.a: No amount of alcohol is good for health
items.why: In a 2022 episode he summarised research showing even moderate drinking harms the brain and body.

items.q: Capital of Chile?
items.why: Founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1541, Santiago has the snowy Andes as a backdrop on clear days.

items.q: Which ancient aqueduct still feeds the Trevi Fountain?
items.why: Legend says a young girl, a 'virgo', showed thirsty soldiers the spring that still feeds it.

items.q: The hormone that tells you you're full?
items.why: Leptin is made by fat cells and signals the brain that energy stores are full.

items.q: Chile's most common beers?
items.why: Both are brewed by CCU, Chile's dominant brewer.

items.q: Who built the Aqua Virgo in 19 BC?
items.why: Marcus Agrippa, Augustus' right-hand man, also built the original Pantheon.

items.q: The hormone that moves glucose from the blood into cells?
items.why: The pancreas releases insulin after a meal so muscles, liver and fat can take up the glucose.

items.q: Roughly how long is Chile from north to south?
items.why: About 4,300 km long but only around 177 km wide on average, from the Atacama Desert to Cape Horn.

items.q: How many major aqueducts eventually supplied ancient Rome?
items.why: Together they delivered enough water for baths, fountains and public toilets across a city of a million people.

items.q: Even 1–2% dehydration can measurably hurt…?
items.why: Small fluid losses are enough to reduce attention, mood and endurance, often before you feel thirsty.

items.q: Valparaíso is famous for…?
items.why: Its hills are covered in painted houses and street art, linked by historic funicular lifts. The centre is UNESCO-listed.

items.q: Which famous three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge is in southern France?
items.why: The 49 m-high bridge near Nîmes was built without mortar, its stones simply cut to fit.

items.q: Finnish studies link sauna use 4–7 times a week to…?
items.why: In a 20-year Finnish study, men using a sauna 4 to 7 times a week had far lower cardiovascular death rates than once-a-week users.

items.q: Valparaíso's hillside funiculars are called…?
items.why: Most date from the late 1800s and early 1900s and still haul people up Valparaíso's steep hills.

items.q: Were most aqueduct channels on tall arches?
wrong: They were all pipes on the surface
items.why: Most of the channels ran underground. The famous arches carried water only across valleys and low ground.

items.q: Regular cold exposure increases which calorie-burning tissue?
items.why: Brown fat is packed with mitochondria that burn energy to make heat. Cold exposure makes you build more of it.

items.q: Which Nobel-winning poet had a house, La Sebastiana, in Valparaíso?
items.why: Neruda had three houses, each crammed with collections: La Sebastiana, La Chascona in Santiago and Isla Negra.

items.q: Which architect designed the Trevi Fountain, finished in 1762?
items.why: Nicola Salvi died before it was finished. It was completed by Giuseppe Pannini in 1762.

items.q: Why does Huberman say to let yourself shiver in cold exposure?
items.why: Shivering muscles release succinate, which signals brown fat to burn energy and make heat.

items.q: The driest non-polar desert on Earth, in northern Chile?
items.why: Some weather stations there have never recorded rain, and NASA tests Mars rover equipment in its soil.

items.q: The tradition at the Trevi Fountain?
items.a: Toss a coin over your shoulder to return to Rome
items.why: The custom is one coin, thrown with the right hand over the left shoulder, to make sure you return.

items.q: How cold should cold exposure be, per Huberman?
items.a: Uncomfortably cold but safe to stay in
wrong: As close to freezing as possible
items.why: Cold enough that you really want to get out, but safe to stay in. There's no prize for going colder.

items.q: Torres del Paine's three granite towers sit in which region?
items.why: The towers are in Magallanes, Chile's southernmost region. The park is famous for its fierce wind.

items.q: Where does the Trevi Fountain coin money go?
items.why: Over a million euros a year is collected and given to Caritas, which uses it to help people in need.

items.q: Huberman's podcast first launched in…?
items.why: Huberman Lab launched in January 2021 and quickly became one of the world's most popular podcasts.

items.q: Chile's remote Pacific island with the moai statues?
items.why: About 3,500 km off Chile, Rapa Nui has around 900 moai, carved by Polynesian settlers.

items.q: Who's the central figure of the Trevi Fountain?
items.why: Oceanus stands in a shell chariot pulled by sea horses, guided by tritons.

items.q: Who's the sleep scientist and author of 'Why We Sleep'?
items.why: Matthew Walker is a neuroscience professor at UC Berkeley. His 2017 book made sleep science mainstream.

items.q: The 1973 coup brought which dictator to power in Chile?
items.why: Pinochet ruled from the 1973 coup until 1990, after losing a 1988 referendum on staying in power.

items.q: What was the Roman Forum?
items.why: Rome's political, religious and commercial centre: temples, law courts, the Senate house and the speakers' platform.

items.q: Chilean slang for 'you know?' or 'got it?'
items.why: From the verb 'cachar', borrowed from English 'catch'. Chileans tag it onto sentences all the time.

items.q: Who rebuilt the Pantheon into its current form around AD 125?
items.why: Hadrian rebuilt it but kept Agrippa's original inscription on the front, which still credits Agrippa.

items.q: Chile and Peru both claim which spirit as their own?
items.why: The name comes from the Peruvian port of Pisco, and both countries protect their own versions.

items.q: What's at the top of the Pantheon's dome?
items.why: The 9 m oculus is the only light source. When it rains, water falls in and drains through holes in the floor.

items.q: Chile's long scenic road through Patagonia?
items.why: Built from 1976, the Carretera Austral winds about 1,200 km through fjords, glaciers and rainforest.

items.q: The Pantheon's dome holds what record?
items.why: Nearly 1,900 years old and 43 m across, it is still the largest dome of unreinforced concrete in the world.

items.q: Capital of Colombia?
items.why: Bogotá sits at about 2,640 m in the Andes, so it's cool all year despite being near the equator.

items.q: Which hill is Rome's legendary founding spot and later the emperors' palace site?
items.why: Emperors built their palaces on the Palatine, which is where the word 'palace' comes from.

items.q: Colombia's most common beers?
items.why: All three are brewed by Bavaria, a company founded in Colombia by German immigrants in 1889.

items.q: Rome's legendary founding year?
items.why: The date was worked out by Roman scholars centuries later. Rome still celebrates its birthday on 21 April.

items.q: Colombia's big hearty platter from the Medellín region?
items.why: Beans, rice, chicharrón, ground meat, chorizo, fried egg, plantain, avocado and arepa: a farmworker's feast.

items.q: Who, in legend, founded Rome after killing his twin?
items.why: In the legend Remus mocked his brother's new city wall by jumping over it, and Romulus killed him.

items.q: Medellín's once-dangerous neighbourhood now famous for graffiti tours and outdoor escalators?
items.why: Once one of Medellín's most violent areas, it was transformed after outdoor escalators arrived in 2011.

items.q: What animal nursed Romulus and Remus?
items.why: The bronze Capitoline Wolf is Rome's emblem. The suckling twins were added during the Renaissance.

items.q: Colombian Nobel winner who wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?
items.why: His 1967 novel set in the town of Macondo defined magical realism. He won the Nobel in 1982.

items.q: What was the Circus Maximus used for?
items.why: The Circus Maximus held perhaps 150,000 people, far more than the Colosseum. Chariot teams had fanatical fans.

items.q: Colombian slang for 'cool'?
items.why: '¡Qué chévere!' and '¡Qué bacano!' both mean 'how great!'. Bacano is especially Colombian.

items.q: When was Julius Caesar assassinated?
items.why: The Ides fell on 15 March. Suetonius says Caesar was stabbed 23 times.

items.q: Colombian slang 'parce' means…?
items.why: Short for 'parcero', partner. In Medellín you'll hear '¿Qué más, parce?' constantly.

items.q: Where exactly was Caesar stabbed?
items.a: In the Curia of Pompey, during a Senate meeting
items.why: The Senate was meeting in a hall in Pompey's theatre complex. The site, Largo di Torre Argentina, is now a cat sanctuary.

items.q: Colombia's famous coffee-growing region?
items.why: The Coffee Axis or Triangle around Manizales, Pereira and Armenia, UNESCO-listed as a cultural landscape.

items.q: Who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC?
items.why: Octavian took the name Augustus, 'revered one', in 27 BC and ruled for about 40 years while keeping a republican front.

items.q: The independence hero, born in Caracas, who liberated Colombia?
items.why: Bolívar's 1819 victory at Boyacá freed Colombia. He dreamed of uniting the continent as Gran Colombia.

items.q: Which river did Caesar cross in 49 BC, starting civil war?
items.why: Roman law forbade generals bringing their armies into Italy. Crossing the little river was a declaration of war.

items.q: The Caribbean coast's mountains, highest coastal range on Earth?
items.why: Its peaks rise to about 5,700 m only around 40 km from the Caribbean beaches near Tayrona.

items.q: Which saying is linked to crossing the Rubicon?
items.why: 'Alea iacta est': once the dice are thrown there's no taking it back. Caesar may actually have quoted it in Greek.

items.q: Colombia is the world's top source of which gemstone?
items.why: Mines like Muzo have produced prized emeralds for centuries, and Colombian stones are famous for their colour.

items.q: Caesar's 'Veni, vidi, vici' boasted of a quick victory where?
items.why: At Zela, in modern Turkey, in 47 BC he crushed Pharnaces II in about five days.

items.q: Capital of Brazil?
items.why: Brasília was planned from scratch, its layout often compared to an aeroplane or a bird with outstretched wings.

items.q: When did the Western Roman Empire fall?
items.why: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last emperor and didn't bother naming another.

items.q: When did Brasília become the capital?
items.why: Built in about 41 months, it moved the capital inland from Rio to open up Brazil's vast interior.

items.q: Who was the last Western Roman emperor, deposed in 476?
items.why: A teenager named after both Rome's founder and its first emperor, which makes the ending rather poetic.

items.q: Architect behind Brasília's modernist buildings and Rio's Sambadrome?
items.why: Niemeyer loved free-flowing curves in concrete and kept working until he died at 104.

items.q: The Eastern Roman Empire lasted until which city fell in 1453?
items.why: The Eastern, or Byzantine, Empire outlived the West by nearly a thousand years until the Ottomans took Constantinople.

items.q: Brazil's language?
items.why: A 1494 treaty gave Portugal the eastern part of South America. Brazil is now the world's largest Portuguese-speaking country.

items.q: Which emperor legalised Christianity in AD 313?
items.why: The Edict of Milan ended persecution of Christians. Constantine later founded Constantinople as a new capital.

items.q: Brazil's most common beers?
items.why: All three belong to AB InBev and are usually served very cold in small bottles or cans.

items.q: Roughly how big was ancient Rome's population at its peak?
items.why: No European city matched that size again until London around 1800.

items.q: Brazil's national cocktail, made with cachaça?
items.why: Cachaça is distilled from fresh sugarcane juice. Muddled with lime and sugar it makes Brazil's classic drink.

items.q: What was Rome's famous 'SPQR'?
items.a: The Senate and People of Rome
items.why: 'Senatus Populusque Romanus'. You can still see SPQR stamped on Rome's manhole covers.

items.q: Brazil's national dish, a black bean and pork stew?
items.why: Black beans slow-cooked with many cuts of pork, traditionally eaten on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

items.q: In what year did Vesuvius bury Pompeii?
items.why: Vesuvius buried Pompeii under metres of ash in AD 79, preserving a Roman town almost frozen in time.

items.q: Largest city in South America?
items.why: São Paulo's metro area has over 20 million people and the largest Japanese community outside Japan.

items.q: Which other town was buried by the same eruption?
items.why: Herculaneum was buried deeper by hot flows that carbonised wood, food and even papyrus scrolls.

items.q: Christ the Redeemer was completed in…?
items.why: The 30 m Art Deco statue was designed by Paul Landowski and built from reinforced concrete and soapstone.

items.q: Who wrote the eyewitness account of the eruption?
items.why: His letters to the historian Tacitus describe the towering cloud, which is why such eruptions are called 'Plinian'.

items.q: Christ the Redeemer stands on which mountain?
items.why: Corcovado means 'hunchback'. A cog railway has carried visitors up since 1884.

items.q: What happened to Pliny the Elder in the eruption?
items.a: He died leading a rescue by sea
items.why: Commander of the fleet at Misenum, he sailed towards the eruption to help and died on the shore at Stabiae.

items.q: Where do Rio's samba schools parade during Carnival?
items.why: Oscar Niemeyer designed the Sambadrome in 1984 as a purpose-built parade avenue lined with stands.

items.q: How were the famous body shapes at Pompeii made?
items.a: Plaster poured into voids left in the ash
items.why: Victims' bodies decayed inside the hardened ash, leaving hollows. Pouring plaster in captured their final poses.

items.q: Florianópolis is mostly on…?
items.why: Most of 'Floripa' is on Santa Catarina Island, which has over 40 beaches.

items.q: Who developed the plaster cast technique in the 1860s?
items.why: Giuseppe Fiorelli, director of the excavations, began making the casts in 1863.

items.q: Brazil's World Cup tally?
items.why: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002, more than any other country.

items.q: What killed most victims at Pompeii?
items.why: Avalanches of superheated gas and ash raced down Vesuvius. Lava played almost no part.

items.q: Which Brazilian surfer won Olympic gold in 2021?
items.why: Italo Ferreira won the first Olympic surfing gold in 2021. He learned to surf on the lid of a polystyrene cooler.

items.q: When did Vesuvius last erupt?
items.why: The 1944 eruption destroyed dozens of Allied bombers parked at a nearby airfield.

items.q: Brazil's wave of world-champion surfers is nicknamed…?
items.why: Brazilian surfers dominated the tour from Gabriel Medina's first world title in 2014.

items.q: Which city sits at the foot of Vesuvius?
items.why: Hundreds of thousands of people live in Vesuvius's official danger zone around Naples.

items.q: Three-time world surfing champion Gabriel Medina is from…?
items.why: Medina won world titles in 2014, 2018 and 2021, and his photo flying above a wave at Tokyo 2020 went viral.

items.q: The traditional date for the eruption is 24 August. What does newer evidence suggest?
items.why: A charcoal graffito dated mid-October and autumn fruits found in the ruins suggest a later eruption date.

items.q: The WSL's Brazil event is usually held at which beach?
items.why: Saquarema is nicknamed the 'Maracanã of surfing' for its powerful beach break.

items.q: What's special about Vatican City's size?
items.why: About 0.44 km², with around 800 residents. You can walk around its walls in under an hour.

items.q: Brazil was a colony of which country?
items.why: Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500. Rio was even the capital of the whole Portuguese Empire from 1808 to 1821.

items.q: Which 1929 treaty made Vatican City an independent state?
items.why: The 1929 treaty settled the 'Roman Question' that began when Italy took Rome from the Pope in 1870.

items.q: Brazil's currency?
items.why: The real arrived in 1994 with a plan that finally ended years of hyperinflation.

items.q: Who signed the Lateran Treaty with the Pope?
wrong: King Victor Emmanuel II in person
items.why: Mussolini's government signed for Italy, and Catholicism became Italy's state religion until 1984.

items.q: Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in…?
items.why: Princess Isabel signed the 'Golden Law' in 1888. Brazil had received more enslaved Africans than any other country.

items.q: Which force guards the Pope, since 1506?
items.why: In the 1527 sack of Rome, 147 Swiss Guards died covering the Pope's escape. Recruits still swear in on 6 May.

items.q: The Brazilian martial art disguised as dance?
items.why: Enslaved Africans developed it, possibly disguising fighting as dance. It's played to the berimbau.

items.q: St Peter's Basilica is built over the traditional tomb of…?
items.why: Excavations in the 1940s found a Roman cemetery under the basilica, where Peter's grave is traditionally placed.

items.q: Capital of Mexico?
items.why: Built on a drained lake bed at about 2,240 m, parts of Mexico City are sinking several centimetres a year.

items.q: Who designed the dome of St Peter's Basilica?
items.why: Michelangelo designed it in his 70s. It was finished after his death by Giacomo della Porta.

items.q: Mexico's best-known beers?
items.a: Corona, Modelo, Tecate and Dos Equis
items.why: Corona, from Grupo Modelo, is Mexico's best-known export beer, sold in well over 100 countries.

items.q: Who designed the great colonnade embracing St Peter's Square?
items.why: Bernini's 284 columns form two arms that symbolically embrace the faithful.

items.q: Tequila must come from which plant?
items.why: Tequila must use blue agave. The cheaper 'mixto' needs only 51%, so look for '100% agave'.

items.q: The huge bronze canopy over St Peter's main altar is Bernini's…?
items.why: About 29 m tall, it's said to use bronze stripped from the Pantheon, which inspired the jibe: 'What the barbarians didn't do, the Barberini did.'

items.q: Tequila mainly comes from which state?
items.why: Most tequila comes from Jalisco, named after the town of Tequila near Guadalajara.

items.q: Which Michelangelo statue in St Peter's is his only signed work?
items.why: He reportedly carved his name on Mary's sash after overhearing visitors credit someone else.

items.q: Mexico's smoky agave spirit, especially from Oaxaca?
items.why: Mezcal's agave hearts are roasted in earth pits, giving the smoke. Technically, tequila is a type of mezcal.

items.q: Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, 1508–1512?
items.why: Michelangelo saw himself as a sculptor, not a painter, and worked standing on scaffolding rather than lying down.

items.q: Spit-roasted pork tacos, brought by Lebanese immigrants?
items.why: Lebanese immigrants brought shawarma. Mexicans swapped in pork, chilli marinade and pineapple.

items.q: Which famous scene on the ceiling shows God and Adam's fingers almost touching?
items.why: Some doctors argue the shape around God resembles a human brain, an apt image for Cerebrito.

items.q: The festival honouring the dead on 1–2 November?
items.why: Families build altars with marigolds, photos and favourite foods to welcome the spirits of the dead home.

items.q: What fresco did Michelangelo later paint on the Sistine altar wall?
items.why: Painted from 1536 to 1541, its nudity caused outrage, and some figures were later covered up.

items.q: Cinco de Mayo marks a victory over which country?
items.why: Mexican forces beat the French at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862. It isn't Mexican Independence Day.

items.q: What signals that a new pope has been elected?
items.why: Ballots are burned after each vote: black smoke means no decision, white smoke from the Sistine Chapel means a new pope.

items.q: Mexico has the largest population of…?
items.why: About 130 million people, more Spanish speakers than Spain has inhabitants twice over.

items.q: The meeting of cardinals that elects a pope is called a…?
items.why: From Latin 'cum clave', with a key: the cardinals are locked in until they choose.

items.q: The Mexican painter famous for self-portraits with a unibrow?
items.why: A bus accident at 18 left her in lifelong pain. Many of her paintings were made from bed.

items.q: Raphael's famous Vatican fresco of Greek philosophers?
items.why: Plato points to the sky and Aristotle gestures at the earth. Plato's face is thought to be modelled on Leonardo.

items.q: Capital of Guatemala?
items.why: Guatemala City became the capital after earthquakes wrecked Antigua in 1773.

items.q: Who was elected pope in May 2025, the first from the United States?
items.why: Robert Prevost was born in Chicago but spent many years as a missionary and bishop in Peru, where he took citizenship.

items.q: Guatemala's currency is named after which bird?
items.why: The resplendent quetzal was sacred to the Maya and is a symbol of liberty.

items.q: Who was the first pope from the Americas, who died in April 2025?
items.why: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, from Buenos Aires, was also the first Jesuit pope. He was elected in 2013.

items.q: Guatemala's most common beer?
items.why: Gallo, 'rooster', has been brewed since 1896 and is a national icon.

items.q: The 1517 protest that split Western Christianity was started by…?
items.why: Luther posted his 95 Theses in Wittenberg in 1517. The printing press spread them across Europe in weeks.

items.q: The colonial former capital ringed by volcanoes?
items.why: Antigua's cobbled streets and ruined churches are a UNESCO site, overlooked by the volcanoes Agua, Fuego and Acatenango.

items.q: What did selling 'indulgences' help fund, angering Luther?
items.why: Preachers like Johann Tetzel sold indulgences, promised time off in purgatory, to raise money for the new St Peter's.

items.q: The hike where you camp watching the next-door volcano erupt?
items.why: From camp on Acatenango you look straight across at Fuego, which erupts every few minutes.

items.q: Years Alcatraz ran as a federal prison?
items.why: It held the country's most troublesome prisoners for 29 years.

items.q: Lake ringed by volcanoes that Aldous Huxley called the world's most beautiful?
items.why: Atitlán fills a huge volcanic caldera, ringed by three volcanoes and Maya villages.

items.q: Alcatraz's nickname?
items.why: 'The Rock' sits about 2 km from San Francisco in the cold, fast waters of the bay.

items.q: Giant Maya city deep in Guatemala's jungle?
items.why: Tikal peaked around AD 200 to 850. Its temples rise above the canopy, and one view appeared in Star Wars.

items.q: Which famous gangster served time on Alcatraz?
items.why: Jailed for tax evasion, Capone spent about four and a half years there, sometimes playing banjo in the prison band.

items.q: Capital of Nicaragua?
items.why: After a 1972 earthquake levelled the centre, many addresses are still given by landmarks, some of which no longer exist.

items.q: The 'Birdman of Alcatraz' was…?
items.why: Robert Stroud studied birds at Leavenworth prison. At Alcatraz he wasn't allowed to keep any.

items.q: Nicaragua's most common beers?
items.why: Toña and Victoria are the two big lagers, ideally drunk ice-cold.

items.q: Who escaped in June 1962 using a raft of raincoats and dummy heads?
items.a: Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers
items.why: They chipped through vents with sharpened spoons over months and paddled off on a raft of glued raincoats.

items.q: Nicaragua's famous rum?
items.why: Flor de Caña has been made since 1890 and is aged at the foot of the San Cristóbal volcano.

items.q: What happened to the 1962 escapees?
items.why: The FBI closed its case in 1979. The US Marshals still keep a file open.

items.q: Where can you go 'volcano boarding'?
items.why: Cerro Negro is Central America's youngest volcano, born in 1850. You hike up and slide down its black gravel on a board.

items.q: What did the 1962 escapees make dummy heads from?
items.a: Soap, toilet paper and real hair
items.why: Lifelike papier-mâché heads in their beds fooled the guards until morning roll call.

items.q: The island in Lake Nicaragua made of two volcanoes?
items.why: Ometepe is formed by the volcanoes Concepción and Maderas, joined by a narrow isthmus.

items.q: Why did Alcatraz close in 1963?
items.a: It was far too expensive to run
items.why: Everything had to be shipped in, and salt air was eating the buildings. It cost about three times more than other federal prisons.

items.q: Nicaragua's currency?
items.why: It's named after Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, the Spaniard who founded Granada and León.

items.q: Why was escape by swimming so dangerous?
items.why: The bay is around 10 to 15 °C with powerful tidal currents, enough to exhaust a swimmer before reaching shore.

items.q: Nicaragua's national dish, also claimed by Costa Rica?
items.why: 'Spotted rooster': rice and beans fried together, eaten at breakfast across Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

items.q: Who occupied Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971?
items.why: The 'Indians of All Tribes' occupation drew national attention to Native American rights.

items.q: Capital of Costa Rica?
items.why: San José sits in the cool Central Valley, ringed by coffee farms and volcanoes.

items.q: Before the prison era, Alcatraz was a…?
items.why: From the 1850s it was a fort guarding San Francisco Bay, then a military prison.

items.q: Costa Rica's national catchphrase?
items.why: 'Pure life' works as hello, thanks, goodbye and a whole philosophy of taking it easy.

items.q: Alcatraz had the first lighthouse on which coast?
items.why: Its lighthouse first shone in 1854.

items.q: What did Costa Rica abolish in 1948?
items.why: After a short civil war, José Figueres abolished the army and put the money into education and health.

items.q: The 1946 two-day standoff on the island is called…?
items.why: An escape attempt in May 1946 turned into a two-day siege. Marines were called in, and five people died.

items.q: Costa Rica's most common beer?
items.why: Imperial's black eagle logo is everywhere, from T-shirts to beach bars.

items.q: How many inmates were officially ever confirmed to have successfully escaped?
items.why: 36 men tried. Most were caught or killed, and the 1962 trio's fate is still unknown.

items.q: Roughly what share of the world's biodiversity is in Costa Rica?
items.why: Roughly 5% of the world's species live on about 0.03% of its land, and around a quarter of the country is protected.

items.q: Which Clint Eastwood film tells the 1962 escape?
items.why: Clint Eastwood played Frank Morris in the 1979 film.

items.q: Costa Rica's famous cone volcano near La Fortuna?
items.why: Arenal erupted in 1968 after centuries of quiet and stayed active until 2010.

items.q: What did the Incas call their empire?
items.why: It means 'the four parts together', the four regions meeting at Cusco. Qhapaq Ñan was their road network.

items.q: Costa Rica's currency?
items.why: The colón is named after Christopher Columbus, Cristóbal Colón in Spanish.

items.q: Capital of the Inca Empire?
items.why: Cusco may mean 'navel' in Quechua: the centre of the Inca world, where the four regions met.

items.q: Capital of Vietnam?
items.why: Hanoi has been a capital since 1010, when it was called Thăng Long, 'ascending dragon'.

items.q: Which Inca ruler began the rapid expansion around 1438?
items.why: His name means roughly 'he who remakes the world'. He turned a small kingdom into an empire.

items.q: Vietnam's largest city?
items.why: Ho Chi Minh City has around 9 million people and even more motorbikes.

items.q: The Incas' main god, the sun?
items.why: The emperor was seen as the son of Inti, and temples to the sun were coated in gold.

items.q: Ho Chi Minh City's old name?
items.why: It was renamed in 1976 after reunification, but most locals still call the centre Saigon.

items.q: Pachamama is…?
items.why: People still offer Pachamama the first drops of a drink, spilled on the ground.

items.q: Vietnam's currency?
items.why: Notes run into the hundreds of thousands, so everyone is briefly a millionaire.

items.q: Instead of writing, the Incas recorded data on knotted cords called…?
items.why: Knots recorded numbers in a base-10 system. Some quipus may also have stored stories, still undeciphered.

items.q: Vietnam's popular beers?
items.a: Bia Hà Nội, Saigon, 333 and Larue
items.why: Bia Hà Nội rules the north and 333 and Saigon the south.

items.q: The Inca road network is called…?
items.why: UNESCO listed the Qhapaq Ñan in 2014 across six countries, from Colombia to Argentina.

items.q: Hanoi's cheap, fresh, unpasteurised street beer?
items.why: Brewed daily and drunk on tiny plastic stools on the pavement for well under a dollar a glass.

items.q: Roughly how long was the Inca road network?
items.why: Amazingly, it was built by a people with no wheeled vehicles or horses.

items.q: Hanoi's famous whipped-yolk drink?
items.why: It was invented at a Hanoi café in 1946, when milk was scarce, by whisking egg yolk and sugar into a cream.

items.q: Inca relay runners who carried messages were called…?
items.why: Relays of runners could carry a message a couple of hundred kilometres in a day. Legend says the emperor got fresh fish from the coast.

items.q: Vietnam's noodle soup, usually beef or chicken?
items.why: Phở came from northern Vietnam in the early 1900s. The broth simmers for hours with star anise and charred ginger.

items.q: The Inca title for the emperor?
items.why: Sapa Inca means 'the only Inca'. He was thought to be descended from the sun.

items.q: Hanoi's grilled pork with noodles dish, eaten by Obama with Anthony Bourdain?
items.why: In 2016 Obama and Anthony Bourdain shared bún chả and beers at a plain Hanoi shop for about $6.

items.q: Which two brothers fought an Inca civil war just before the Spanish arrived?
items.why: Atahualpa had just won the civil war when Pizarro arrived, leaving the empire divided and weakened.

items.q: Vietnam's limestone-island bay, a UNESCO site?
items.why: Around 1,600 limestone islands rise from the bay. Its name means 'descending dragon'.

items.q: What killed Emperor Huayna Cápac, triggering the succession war?
items.a: Smallpox that spread ahead of the Spanish
items.why: Smallpox raced ahead of the Spanish through trade routes around 1528, killing the emperor and his heir and sparking civil war.

items.q: The lantern-lit ancient trading town in central Vietnam?
items.why: A busy port from the 1400s to the 1700s. On full-moon nights the old town switches off its lights for lanterns.

items.q: Inca stonework is famous because…?
items.why: Stones were shaped to fit so tightly that a knife blade won't slip between them, and the joints flex in earthquakes.

items.q: The underground network used by Viet Cong fighters near Saigon?
items.why: The Viet Cong dug about 250 km of tunnels with kitchens, hospitals and meeting rooms.

items.q: Inca 'Inti Raymi' is the festival of…?
items.a: The sun, at the winter solstice
items.why: June is winter in the Andes. Banned by the Spanish, the festival was revived in 1944 and is staged at Sacsayhuamán.

items.q: The Vietnam War ended with the fall of Saigon in…?
items.why: North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon on 30 April 1975, ending the war.

items.q: Where was Francisco Pizarro from?
items.why: Trujillo in Extremadura, a poor region that produced many conquistadors.

items.q: Vietnam's 1954 victory that ended French colonial rule?
items.why: The siege of Dien Bien Phu in 1954 ended French Indochina, and Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel.

items.q: On which island did Pizarro draw his famous line in the sand in 1527?
items.why: Stuck on Isla del Gallo off Colombia's coast in 1527, he drew his line and asked who would go on.

items.q: Vietnamese is unusual in Asia for using…?
items.why: The Latin-based script, Quốc ngữ, was developed by European missionaries in the 1600s.

items.q: What did Pizarro say as he drew the line, roughly?
items.a: Peru and riches, or Panama and poverty
wrong: For God and Spain, follow me
items.why: On Isla del Gallo in 1527 he drew a line in the sand: cross it for Peru and riches, or go back to Panama and poverty.

items.q: The famous motorbike loop in Vietnam's far north?
items.why: The loop winds through limestone mountains near China, including the dramatic Mã Pí Lèng Pass.

items.q: How many men crossed the line to stay with Pizarro?
items.why: They became known as 'los Trece de la Fama', the Famous Thirteen.

items.q: Capital of Thailand?
items.why: Thais call it Krung Thep, 'city of angels'.

items.q: Who was Pizarro's partner in the early Peru expeditions, later his rival?
items.why: They fell out over who got Cusco. Pizarro's brothers executed Almagro in 1538.

items.q: Thailand's currency?
items.why: The baht started as a unit of weight for silver, and gold is still sold by the baht.

items.q: Which 1529 agreement with the Spanish Crown licensed Pizarro to conquer Peru?
items.why: Signed in Toledo in 1529, it named Pizarro governor of the lands he hoped to conquer.

items.q: Thailand's best-known beers?
items.why: Singha has been brewed since 1933. Chang, with its elephants, is the cheaper and stronger rival.

items.q: Was the conquest mainly paid for by the King of Spain?
items.why: The Crown granted rights and took a fifth of the treasure, but investors and the conquistadors themselves paid the costs.

items.q: What's unique about Thailand's history in Southeast Asia?
items.a: It was never colonised by a European power
items.why: Siam was a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina, and shrewd kings modernised to keep it independent.

items.q: Roughly how many Spaniards were with Pizarro at Cajamarca in 1532?
items.why: About 168 men, 62 of them on horseback, faced an Inca army of tens of thousands.

items.q: Thailand's April new-year water fight festival?
items.why: Songkran, 13 to 15 April, began as a gentle sprinkling of water for blessing. Now it's a nationwide water fight.

items.q: Which Inca emperor did Pizarro capture at Cajamarca?
items.why: In November 1532 the Spanish ambushed Atahualpa's unarmed escort in Cajamarca's square and seized him.

items.q: The festival of floating lanterns and baskets in November?
items.why: People float little banana-leaf baskets with candles on rivers. In Chiang Mai it coincides with Yi Peng sky lanterns.

items.q: Why were horses such a shock to the Incas?
items.a: They'd never seen horses, and cavalry was devastating
wrong: Horses were forbidden in the Andes
items.why: The biggest Andean animal was the llama, which can't be ridden, so mounted charges were terrifying.

items.q: Thailand's national sport, 'the art of eight limbs'?
items.why: The eight limbs are fists, elbows, knees and shins.

items.q: What ransom did Atahualpa offer for his release?
items.why: One room of gold and two of silver. It was paid, and Pizarro executed him anyway in 1533.

items.q: Thailand's spicy, sour prawn soup?
items.why: Lemongrass, galangal, lime leaves and chilli give tom yum its hot and sour kick.

items.q: What happened to Atahualpa after the ransom was paid?
items.why: He was garrotted in July 1533, after being baptised to avoid being burned.

items.q: Bangkok's full ceremonial name holds what record?
items.why: The ceremonial name runs to 168 letters in its romanised form. Thais shorten it to Krung Thep.

items.q: How did Pizarro die in 1541?
items.a: Assassinated in Lima by Almagro's supporters
items.why: Followers of Almagro's son broke into his Lima palace in 1541 to avenge the elder Almagro.

items.q: Thailand's northern 'rose of the north' city?
items.why: Founded in 1296 as capital of the Lanna kingdom, Chiang Mai has over 300 temples.

items.q: Which city did Pizarro found in 1535 as the new capital?
items.why: He chose the coast so the capital could be reached by sea from Panama and Spain.

items.q: Thailand's current king, crowned 2019?
items.why: King Vajiralongkorn, Rama X, succeeded his father Bhumibol, who reigned for 70 years.

items.q: Besides steel and horses, what most helped the Spanish beat the Incas?
items.a: Disease and the Inca civil war
items.why: Epidemics had killed huge numbers and a civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar had split the empire. Pizarro arrived at the perfect moment.

items.q: Thailand was called what until 1939?
items.why: Siam was renamed Thailand, 'land of the free', in 1939.

items.q: Which Inca leader led a long resistance from Vilcabamba after the conquest?
items.why: Installed as a puppet ruler, Manco Inca rebelled in 1536 and then fought on from the jungle at Vilcabamba.

items.q: Bali belongs to which country?
items.why: Bali is one of about 38 Indonesian provinces, with around 4 million people.

items.q: Who was the last Inca ruler, executed in 1572?
items.why: Túpac Amaru was executed in Cusco's main square in 1572. A rebel leader took his name in 1780.

items.q: Indonesia's capital?
items.why: A new capital, Nusantara, is being built on Borneo because Jakarta is sinking and overcrowded.

items.q: Cusco was laid out in the shape of which animal?
items.why: Pachacuti is said to have planned Cusco in the shape of a puma, a symbol of strength and the earthly world.

items.q: Bali's main religion, unusual in Indonesia?
items.why: Most Balinese practise their own form of Hinduism, while Indonesia as a whole is mostly Muslim.

items.q: Which fortress forms the puma's head in Cusco's layout?
items.why: Its zigzag walls are said to be the puma's teeth. Some stones weigh over 100 tonnes.

items.q: Indonesia's most common beer?
items.why: Bintang, 'star', descends from a Heineken brewery of the Dutch colonial era.

items.q: Cusco's Inca sun temple, later topped by a Spanish convent?
items.why: Its walls were sheathed in gold. In the 1950 earthquake the Spanish convent cracked but the Inca walls held.

items.q: Indonesia's currency?
items.why: With tens of thousands of rupiah to the dollar, everyday prices have a lot of zeros.

items.q: Altitude of Cusco?
items.why: About 3,400 m. Travellers sip coca tea and take it slow for the first days.

items.q: Bali's 'Day of Silence', when the whole island shuts down?
items.why: On Nyepi even the airport closes. No lights, no work, no travel: a day for reflection.

items.q: The Sacred Valley follows which river?
items.why: The Urubamba, or Vilcanota, flows past Machu Picchu and on into the Amazon basin.

items.q: Bali's famous sunrise volcano trek?
items.why: Climbers start in the dark to watch the sun rise behind Mount Agung from Batur's rim.

items.q: Circular terraces in the Sacred Valley thought to be an Inca crop lab?
items.why: Each terrace has its own microclimate, with big temperature differences from top to bottom: ideal for testing crops.

items.q: Bali's highest and most sacred volcano?
items.why: At about 3,031 m, Agung is home to Besakih, Bali's mother temple. Its 1963 eruption killed over a thousand people.

items.q: Hillside salt pools used since before the Incas?
items.why: Thousands of pools are fed by a salty spring. Local families still own and harvest them.

items.q: Bali's spit-roasted suckling pig?
items.why: Babi guling is stuffed with spices and turned over a fire, a Balinese ceremonial dish.

items.q: Sacred Valley town with a fortress where the Incas beat the Spanish in 1537?
items.why: In 1537 Manco Inca flooded the plain and drove off the Spanish. Ollantaytambo is still a living Inca town.

items.q: Bali's arts-and-rice-terraces town?
items.why: Ubud's rice terraces use subak, a centuries-old cooperative irrigation system listed by UNESCO.

items.q: The three Inca sacred animals and their worlds: condor (heavens), puma (earth) and…?
items.why: Snake for the underworld, puma for this world and condor for the heavens: the three realms of Andean belief.

items.q: Bali's clifftop temple and surf spot in the south?
items.why: Uluwatu Temple sits on a 70 m cliff. Kecak fire dances are performed there at sunset.

items.q: Machu Picchu was most likely built as an estate for which emperor?
items.why: It was probably a royal estate and religious retreat for Pachacuti, the emperor who built the empire.

items.q: Roughly how many islands make up Indonesia?
items.why: Fewer than 7,000 of its islands are inhabited, spread across a span wider than Australia.

items.q: Roughly when was Machu Picchu built?
items.why: Built around 1450, it was occupied for less than a century before being abandoned.

items.q: The world's largest Muslim-majority country by population?
items.why: Indonesia has well over 200 million Muslims, more than any other country.

items.q: Who brought Machu Picchu to world attention in 1911?
items.why: Locals farming the terraces guided the Yale lecturer there. Bingham called it a 'lost city'; it wasn't lost to them.

items.q: Capital of Laos?
items.why: Vientiane's Patuxai monument was famously built with American cement meant for an airport runway.

items.q: Did the Spanish ever find Machu Picchu?
items.why: The Spanish never found it, so it escaped the looting and destruction that hit other Inca sites.

items.q: Laos's dominant beer?
items.why: Brewed with local jasmine rice, Beerlao is a point of national pride.

items.q: The peak that looms behind the classic Machu Picchu photo?
items.why: Huayna Picchu, 'young mountain', has a steep path to temple ruins at the top.

items.q: Laos's currency?
items.why: Thousands of kip make a dollar. Thai baht and US dollars are often accepted too.

items.q: Machu Picchu was voted one of the New Seven Wonders in…?
items.why: A worldwide public vote in 2007 named it one of the New Seven Wonders.

items.q: Laos's grim world record from the Vietnam War era?
items.a: Most heavily bombed country per capita in history
items.why: The US dropped over 2 million tonnes of bombs on Laos from 1964 to 1973, about one planeload every eight minutes for nine years.

items.q: What does 'Machu Picchu' mean?
items.why: It's named after the mountain on the other side of the ruins from Huayna Picchu, the 'young mountain'.

items.q: Roughly how many cluster bomblets were dropped on Laos?
items.why: About a third failed to explode. Unexploded bombs still injure people today, and clearance will take decades.

items.q: The famous gateway on the Inca Trail with the first view of Machu Picchu?
wrong: The Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku
items.why: Inca Trail hikers reach Intipunku at dawn on their final day for their first view of the ruins below.

items.q: Laos's UNESCO town famous for the dawn monks' alms-giving?
items.why: At dawn, saffron-robed monks file through the streets to receive sticky rice. Visitors should watch quietly.

items.q: The Aztec capital, built on a lake island in 1325?
items.why: Linked to the shore by causeways, Tenochtitlan had perhaps 200,000 people, bigger than any city in Spain at the time.

items.q: The turquoise multi-tiered waterfalls near Luang Prabang?
items.why: Limestone in the water makes the turquoise pools, and a bear rescue centre sits at the entrance.

items.q: What sign told the Aztecs where to build their capital?
items.a: An eagle on a cactus eating a snake
items.why: Their god Huitzilopochtli told them to settle where they saw this sign. They found it on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco.

items.q: Laos's staple, eaten by hand in balls?
items.why: Laos eats more sticky rice per person than anywhere, rolled into balls by hand and dipped in sauces.

items.q: Where does that eagle-cactus-snake image appear today?
items.why: The image sits at the centre of Mexico's flag and coat of arms.

items.q: Laos's minced meat and herb 'salad', a national dish?
items.why: Minced meat with lime, fish sauce, herbs and toasted rice powder for crunch.

items.q: Modern city built on top of Tenochtitlan?
items.why: The Spanish built over the ruins. Remains of the Templo Mayor were rediscovered beside the cathedral in 1978.

items.q: Is Laos landlocked?
items.a: Yes, the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia
wrong: No, it has a short coast
items.why: The Mekong River is its lifeline for trade and travel.

items.q: Spanish conquistador who toppled the Aztecs in 1521?
items.why: Cortés had a few hundred Spaniards but tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, especially the Tlaxcalans.

items.q: Laos's famous river-tubing backpacker town?
items.why: After deaths in 2012 the riverside bars were closed. Today it's known for karst scenery and hot-air balloons.

items.q: Aztec emperor when Cortés arrived?
items.why: Moctezuma II welcomed Cortés into the city in 1519 and died in Spanish custody the next year.

items.q: Sri Lanka's official legislative capital?
items.why: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the official capital and seat of parliament. Colombo, next door, is the commercial capital.

items.q: Language of the Aztecs, still spoken by over a million Mexicans?
items.why: Nahuatl is still spoken by about 1.7 million people in Mexico.

items.q: Sri Lanka's biggest city and commercial capital?
items.why: Colombo is the commercial hub and main port. Parliament sits next door in Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte.

items.q: Everyday English words from Nahuatl?
items.why: From xocolatl, tomatl, ahuacatl and chīlli. Coyote and chipotle come from Nahuatl too.

items.q: Sri Lanka's two main languages?
items.why: Both are official languages. Sinhala speakers are the majority and Tamil speakers live mostly in the north and east.

items.q: The Aztec sun and war god, fed with human sacrifice?
items.why: Huitzilopochtli shared the top of the Templo Mayor with the rain god Tlaloc.

items.q: Sri Lanka's old name until 1972?
items.why: It became Sri Lanka, 'resplendent island', in 1972, though Ceylon tea kept the old name.

items.q: The feathered serpent god?
items.why: Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, was worshipped across Mesoamerica. The Maya called him Kukulkan.

items.q: Sri Lanka's best-known beer?
items.why: Lion has been brewed since 1881, originally for British planters in the hill country.

items.q: Ancient city near Mexico City with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon?
items.why: At its peak around AD 450 Teotihuacan may have had over 100,000 people. Its Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest in the Americas.

items.q: The giant rock fortress with ancient frescoes?
items.why: King Kashyapa built a palace on top of the 200 m rock in the 5th century, entered between giant lion's paws.

items.q: Did the Aztecs build Teotihuacan?
items.a: No, it was already ancient ruins to them
items.why: Teotihuacan peaked around AD 450 and was abandoned centuries before the Aztecs arrived. They named it 'place where gods were born'.

items.q: Kandy's temple holds which relic?
items.why: The relic is paraded through Kandy during the Esala Perahera festival, with elephants and dancers.

items.q: Teotihuacan's main avenue?
items.why: The Aztecs named it, believing the platforms along it were tombs. They were actually temples and palaces.

items.q: The famous railway viaduct near Ella?
items.why: Completed in 1921 from brick and stone, a popular story says the steel meant for it went to the First World War.

items.q: The step pyramid of El Castillo is at which Maya site?
items.why: Its four stairways of 91 steps plus the top platform add up to 365, one for each day of the year.

items.q: Sri Lanka's world-famous export crop?
items.why: When disease wiped out coffee in the 1870s, planters switched to tea, and Ceylon tea became world-famous.

items.q: What happens at El Castillo at the equinoxes?
items.a: Shadows form a serpent sliding down the stairs
wrong: The sun sets through the top
items.why: Late-afternoon sun throws triangles of shadow down the steps that join the carved serpent head at the bottom.

items.q: Sri Lanka gave the world its first…?
items.why: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became prime minister in 1960.

items.q: Which pyramid has the largest volume of any in the world?
items.a: The Great Pyramid of Cholula, Mexico
items.why: Cholula is so overgrown it looks like a hill, with a Spanish church on top. By volume it beats Giza.

items.q: Sri Lanka's currency?
items.why: The rupee crashed in the 2022 economic crisis, which brought down the government.

items.q: Which civilisation built Chichén Itzá, Tikal and Palenque?
items.why: The Maya developed writing, astronomy and a precise calendar. Millions of Maya people still live in the region.

items.q: Capital of England and the UK?
items.why: The Romans founded Londinium around AD 47 at a good crossing point on the Thames.

items.q: The 'mother culture' of Mexico famed for giant stone heads?
items.why: The Olmecs flourished from about 1200 BC. Their basalt heads stand up to about 3 m tall and weigh many tonnes.

items.q: The UK's best-selling lager?
items.why: Despite being a British staple, Carling started out as a Canadian beer.

items.q: When did the Berlin Wall go up?
items.why: Berliners woke on 13 August 1961 to find barbed wire across their streets. Concrete followed within days.

items.q: The 1215 charter that limited the English king's power?
items.why: Barons forced King John to seal it at Runnymede. Four original copies survive.

items.q: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
items.why: It's not a national holiday because 9 November is also the anniversary of Kristallnacht.

items.q: 'Big Ben' is actually the name of…?
items.why: The 13.7-tonne bell is Big Ben. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

items.q: When was Germany officially reunified?
items.why: 3 October is now the Day of German Unity, Germany's national day.

items.q: The 1066 invasion that changed English history?
items.why: After 1066 the elite spoke French for centuries, which is why English has 'beef' alongside 'cow'.

items.q: Who built the Berlin Wall?
items.why: East Germany built it with Soviet approval. Families were split overnight.

items.q: Who won the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
items.why: King Harold was killed, famously shown with an arrow in his eye on the Bayeux Tapestry.

items.q: The GDR's official name for the Wall?
items.why: 'Antifaschistischer Schutzwall': the regime claimed it kept fascists out. Everyone knew it kept people in.

items.q: The prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain?
items.why: Built in stages from about 3000 BC, some of its stones were dragged from Wales, over 200 km away. It aligns with the solstices.

items.q: The real reason the Wall was built?
items.a: To stop East Germans fleeing to the West
items.why: Around 3.5 million East Germans had fled west by 1961. The GDR called it an anti-fascist rampart, but it faced inward.

items.q: Henry VIII broke from the Pope mainly to…?
items.why: When the Pope refused an annulment, Henry made himself head of the Church of England in 1534.

items.q: Roughly how many people were killed at the Wall?
items.why: Research by the Berlin Wall memorial counts at least 140 people killed at the Wall or dying in connection with it between 1961 and 1989.

items.q: Britain's longest-reigning monarch?
items.why: Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years, from 1952 until 2022.

items.q: The 'death strip' was…?
items.why: A raked sand strip with watchtowers, lights and guards between the inner and outer walls, so escapers could be seen and shot.

items.q: Current UK monarch?
items.why: Charles III became king in September 2022, aged 73, the oldest person to take the British throne.

items.q: The famous Allied crossing point between East and West Berlin?
items.why: 'Charlie' is C in the military alphabet. In 1961 US and Soviet tanks faced off there for 16 hours.

items.q: The UK's currency?
items.why: Sterling is the world's oldest currency still in use, dating back over 1,200 years.

items.q: The longest surviving stretch of the Wall, covered in murals?
items.why: Artists painted about 1.3 km of the Wall in 1990, including the famous Brezhnev-Honecker kiss.

items.q: Capital of Norway?
items.why: Oslo was called Christiania for about 300 years until 1925.

items.q: JFK's famous 1963 Berlin line?
items.why: Kennedy declared solidarity with West Berlin in June 1963. The 'jelly doughnut' joke about it is a myth.

items.q: Norway's currency?
items.why: Norway kept its krone and stayed out of the euro, like the EU itself.

items.q: Who said 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' in 1987?
items.why: Reagan spoke at the Brandenburg Gate in June 1987. Two years later the Wall was open.

items.q: Norway's popular beers?
items.why: Aass, brewed in Drammen since 1834, is Norway's oldest brewery.

items.q: What triggered the Wall opening on 9 November 1989?
items.why: Spokesman Günter Schabowski said new travel rules applied 'immediately'. Crowds rushed the checkpoints and the guards gave way.

items.q: Is Norway in the EU?
items.why: Norwegians voted no in 1972 and 1994 but trade with the EU through the European Economic Area.

items.q: After WWII, Berlin was split into how many occupation sectors?
items.why: American, British, French and Soviet sectors. Berlin sat deep inside the Soviet zone.

items.q: Norway's oil fund holds what title?
items.why: Oil and gas money is invested abroad for future generations. The fund is worth well over a trillion dollars.

items.q: The 1948–49 operation that flew supplies into blockaded West Berlin?
items.why: Over about 15 months, Allied planes flew some 270,000 flights to feed the city. Some pilots dropped sweets for children.

items.q: The Norwegian who first reached the South Pole in 1911?
items.why: Amundsen beat Robert Scott's team by about five weeks, using sled dogs and skis.

items.q: Where was Adolf Hitler born?
items.why: He was born in Braunau am Inn, Austria, in 1889 and later moved to Germany.

items.q: Which Nobel Prize is awarded in Oslo?
items.why: Nobel's will gave the Peace Prize to a Norwegian committee. The other prizes are awarded in Stockholm.

items.q: When did Hitler become Chancellor of Germany?
items.why: President Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933. Within months the Nazis had dismantled democracy.

items.q: Norway's flat-topped cliff over Lysefjord?
items.why: The flat rock juts 604 m straight above Lysefjord.

items.q: Hitler's failed 1923 coup attempt in Munich?
wrong: The Night of the Long Knives
items.why: The November 1923 coup failed and Hitler was jailed, but the trial made him nationally known.

items.q: Norway's sweet, caramel-coloured cheese?
items.why: Brunost is made by boiling whey until its sugars caramelise. It's sliced thin with a special cheese slicer.

items.q: The book Hitler wrote in prison?
items.why: He dictated it in Landsberg prison after the failed putsch. It set out his racist worldview.

items.q: The UNESCO fjord famous for the Seven Sisters waterfall?
items.why: Across the fjord from the Seven Sisters is a waterfall called the Suitor, said to be wooing them.

items.q: The 1938 night of violent attacks on Jewish homes and synagogues?
wrong: The Night of the Long Knives
items.why: 'Night of broken glass', 9 to 10 November 1938, when synagogues, homes and shops were attacked across Germany.

items.q: Norway's famous seafaring raiders of 793–1066?
