items.why: The Viking age is usually dated from the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 to the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066.

items.q: Roughly how many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
items.why: About six million Jews were murdered, roughly two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population.

items.q: Capital of Denmark?
items.why: Copenhagen means 'merchants' harbour'.

items.q: The largest Nazi death camp?
items.why: About 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz. Its liberation date, 27 January, is Holocaust Memorial Day.

items.q: Denmark's currency?
items.why: Danes voted to keep the krone in a 2000 referendum, though it's tightly pegged to the euro.

items.q: How and where did Hitler die?
items.a: Suicide in his Berlin bunker, 30 April 1945
items.why: He killed himself in his bunker on 30 April 1945 as Soviet troops closed in. Germany surrendered a week later.

items.q: Denmark's famous beer brands?
items.why: Carlsberg dates from 1847. It merged with its old rival Tuborg in 1970.

items.q: The post-war trials of leading Nazis were held in…?
items.why: The trials in 1945 and 1946 established that following orders was no defence for crimes against humanity.

items.q: LEGO's name comes from Danish 'leg godt', meaning…?
items.why: Carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen founded LEGO in Billund in 1932, starting with wooden toys.

items.q: The samurai code of honour?
items.why: 'The way of the warrior' stressed loyalty, courage and honour. It was mostly codified during the peaceful Edo period.

items.q: The Danish idea of cosy contentment?
items.why: Candles, blankets, good company: a big part of how Danes cope with long, dark winters.

items.q: A samurai without a master was a…?
items.why: Ronin means 'wave man', drifting like a wave, a disgraced status after a master's death or fall.

items.q: Copenhagen's 1843 amusement park that inspired Walt Disney?
items.why: Walt Disney visited Tivoli in the 1950s, and it helped shape his plans for Disneyland.

items.q: The paired swords a samurai wore, katana and wakizashi?
items.why: Daishō means 'big-little'. Wearing the pair was the badge of the samurai class.

items.q: Copenhagen's statue based on a Hans Christian Andersen tale?
items.why: Unveiled in 1913, the statue is only about 1.25 m tall. It has been vandalised and even beheaded.

items.q: The special steel smelted for katanas?
items.why: Tamahagane was smelted from iron sand in a clay tatara furnace over days of continuous firing.

items.q: Denmark's open sandwich?
items.why: Dense rye bread topped with herring, egg, roast beef or shrimp, eaten with a knife and fork.

items.q: Why do katanas have a curve and a wavy line, the hamon?
items.a: Clay-coated differential hardening: hard edge, flexible spine
wrong: They're bent by hand after forging
items.why: A thicker clay coat on the spine kept it softer while the edge cooled fast and hard. The edge's expansion helps create the curve.

items.q: Denmark's flag, the Dannebrog, is known as…?
items.a: The oldest national flag in use
items.why: Legend dates it to 1219. It's widely cited as the oldest continuously used national flag.

items.q: Why was katana steel folded many times?
items.why: Tamahagane steel from a clay furnace was uneven. Folding spread carbon evenly and drove out slag.

items.q: Copenhagen's colourful canal-side harbour?
items.why: Hans Christian Andersen lived at Nyhavn for years.

items.q: Ritual suicide by disembowelment?
items.why: Also known as harakiri, it let a samurai die with honour rather than be captured or disgraced.

items.q: Capital of Sweden?
items.why: Stockholm is spread across islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic, earning it the nickname 'Venice of the North'.

items.q: The undefeated swordsman who wrote The Book of Five Rings?
items.why: Musashi claimed over 60 duels undefeated. He reportedly beat Sasaki Kojirō with a wooden sword carved from an oar.

items.q: Sweden's currency?
items.why: Swedes voted against the euro in 2003, so the krona stayed.

items.q: The 1600 battle that put the Tokugawa in power?
items.why: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara in 1600 led to over 250 years of peace under his family's rule.

items.q: Sweden's popular beers?
items.why: Carlsberg is Danish, Lapin Kulta Finnish and Ringnes Norwegian.

items.q: The shogun who founded the Tokugawa shogunate?
items.why: Ieyasu became shogun in 1603. His family ruled from Edo, now Tokyo, until 1868.

items.q: The Swedish coffee-and-cake break?
items.why: Fika is a sacred daily break for coffee and something sweet, often a cinnamon bun.

items.q: The African man who became a samurai under Oda Nobunaga?
items.why: Yasuke arrived with Jesuit missionaries in 1579 and became a retainer of the warlord Oda Nobunaga.

items.q: Sweden's state-run liquor store monopoly?
items.why: Only Systembolaget may sell drinks over 3.5% alcohol in shops, and it closes early, to curb heavy drinking.

items.q: What ended the samurai class in the 1870s?
items.why: Japan modernised rapidly after 1868, and in 1876 samurai were banned from carrying swords in public.

items.q: The warship that sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, now a museum?
items.why: The top-heavy Vasa sank barely 1,300 m into its voyage. Raised in 1961, it's about 98% original.

items.q: Samurai leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion, inspiration for The Last Samurai?
items.why: Saigō Takamori led the last samurai revolt in 1877 and died at the Battle of Shiroyama.

items.q: Stockholm is spread across how many islands?
items.why: The city sits on 14 islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic, joined by over 50 bridges.

items.q: The 47 Ronin are famous for…?
items.a: Avenging their master, then committing seppuku
items.why: In 1703 they avenged their lord's forced suicide. Their graves at Sengaku-ji in Tokyo still draw visitors.

items.q: Famous Swedish companies?
items.why: For a country of about 10 million, Sweden has produced a remarkable list of global brands.

items.q: Which typhoons destroyed Mongol invasion fleets in 1274 and 1281?
items.why: The storms saved Japan twice. In WWII the name was given to suicide pilots.

items.q: The Swedish pop band that won Eurovision in 1974 with 'Waterloo'?
items.why: ABBA won in Brighton in 1974 and became one of the best-selling acts in music history.

items.q: Capital of China?
items.why: Beijing means 'northern capital'. It has been China's capital for most of the last 800 years.

items.q: The Swede whose will created the Nobel Prizes?
items.why: The inventor of dynamite left most of his fortune to fund the prizes, first awarded in 1901.

items.q: Which city is home to the Terracotta Army?
items.why: Xi'an, once Chang'an, was the capital of several dynasties and the eastern end of the Silk Road.

items.q: Capital of Germany?
items.why: Bonn was West Germany's capital. Parliament voted in 1991 to move back to Berlin.

items.q: Who were the Terracotta Warriors made to guard?
items.why: Qin Shi Huang, who unified China in 221 BC, was buried with an army of over 8,000 clay soldiers, each with a unique face.

items.q: Germany's best-selling beers include…?
items.why: Germany has well over a thousand breweries, so even its biggest brands have modest national shares.

items.q: Who discovered the Terracotta Army in 1974?
items.why: In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi'an struck clay fragments. Thousands of soldiers lay beneath.

items.q: The 1516 Bavarian beer purity law?
items.why: Issued in 1516, it's often called the oldest food-quality law still referenced today.

items.q: Most of the Great Wall you see today was built under which dynasty?
items.why: The brick-and-stone wall in photos is mostly Ming, built after the Mongols were driven out in 1368.

items.q: Under the purity law beer could contain only water, barley and…?
items.why: The 1516 Reinheitsgebot named only water, barley and hops. Yeast was added once people understood fermentation.

items.q: Can you see the Great Wall from space with the naked eye?
items.why: It's long but only a few metres wide and the same colour as the land around it. Astronauts confirm you can't pick it out.

items.q: Munich's beer festival actually starts in which month?
items.why: The first Oktoberfest celebrated a royal wedding in October 1810. It moved earlier to catch warmer weather.

items.q: The Beijing palace complex closed to commoners for 500 years?
items.why: Home to 24 emperors over nearly 500 years, its roughly 980 buildings form the world's largest palace complex.

items.q: Berlin's signature street snack?
items.why: Legend credits Herta Heuwer in 1949, who mixed ketchup and curry powder from British soldiers.

items.q: China's Four Great Inventions: paper, printing, the compass and…?
items.why: Gunpowder was reportedly discovered by alchemists searching for an elixir of immortality.

items.q: The neoclassical gate that became a symbol of division and reunification?
items.why: Built in 1791, the gate stood in the death strip behind the Wall, then became the symbol of reunification.

items.q: Who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949?
items.why: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949 after winning the civil war.

items.q: Germany's parliament building with a glass dome?
items.why: Norman Foster's glass dome opened in 1999. Visitors can walk above the debating chamber, a symbol of transparency.

items.q: China's best-known beer?
items.why: Tsingtao was founded in 1903 by German settlers in the port city of Qingdao.

items.q: Capital of Spain?
items.why: Philip II made Madrid capital in 1561, partly because it sits near the geographic centre of Spain.

items.q: The ancient trade network linking China to the Mediterranean?
items.why: Silk, spices, ideas and religions travelled along it. The name was coined by a German geographer in 1877.

items.q: Spain's popular beers?
items.why: Also Estrella Galicia and Cruzcampo. Super Bock and Sagres are Portuguese, Peroni Italian, Quilmes Argentine.

items.q: The ancient Chinese general who wrote The Art of War?
items.why: His most quoted advice: know your enemy and know yourself, and you need not fear a hundred battles.

items.q: Paella originally comes from which region?
items.why: Traditional Valencian paella uses chicken, rabbit and green beans. The crispy crust at the bottom is the socarrat.

items.q: WWI years?
items.why: About 9 million soldiers died. Contemporaries called it 'the war to end all wars'.

items.q: Gaudí's unfinished basilica, begun in 1882?
items.why: Gaudí worked on it for over 40 years until his death in 1926. Construction continues, funded by visitors.

items.q: Whose assassination in Sarajevo triggered WWI?
items.why: The heir to Austria-Hungary was shot on 28 June 1914. Alliances turned a regional crisis into a world war within weeks.

items.q: Granada's Moorish palace-fortress?
items.why: Built by the Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim rulers in Spain until Granada fell in 1492.

items.q: Who shot Franz Ferdinand?
items.why: Princip was a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb. He had a chance shot after the archduke's driver took a wrong turn.

items.q: The dictator who ruled Spain from 1939 to 1975?
items.why: Franco won the 1936 to 1939 civil war. After his death, Spain moved to democracy under King Juan Carlos.

items.q: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and…?
items.why: The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in late 1914. Its defeat led to its break-up.

items.q: The tomato-throwing festival in Buñol?
items.why: Held on the last Wednesday of August, it began with a street brawl in 1945 and now draws thousands.

items.q: The main Allies (Entente) at the start of WWI?
items.why: The Triple Entente were bound by a web of agreements, joined later by Italy, the US and others.

items.q: Pamplona's running of the bulls festival?
items.why: Held from 6 to 14 July, Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' made it world-famous.

items.q: Which country switched to the Allied side in 1915?
items.why: Britain and France promised Italy territory in the secret 1915 Treaty of London.

items.q: Besides Spanish, which language is spoken around Barcelona?
items.why: Catalan is an official language in Catalonia, used in schools, signs and parliament.

items.q: When did the USA join WWI?
items.why: Unrestricted German submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram brought the US in, in April 1917.

items.q: The 1492 voyage sponsored by Spain's monarchs?
items.a: Columbus's first voyage to the Americas
items.why: Columbus landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, convinced he had reached Asia.

items.q: Which country left WWI after its 1917 revolution?
items.why: After the Bolshevik Revolution, Russia signed a separate peace at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918.

items.q: Spain's cured ham from acorn-fed black pigs?
items.why: The best, 'de bellota', comes from black Iberian pigs fattened on acorns and cured for years.

items.q: The 1915 campaign where the ANZACs landed in Turkey?
items.why: The landings began on 25 April 1915. After eight months the Allies withdrew.

items.q: Capital of Portugal?
items.why: Lisbon is one of the oldest cities in western Europe, older than Rome by some accounts.

items.q: Anzac Day is on which date?
items.why: Dawn services mark the hour of the Gallipoli landings in Australia and New Zealand.

items.q: Portugal's two big beers?
items.why: Super Bock is the Porto favourite and Sagres the Lisbon one, a friendly national rivalry.

items.q: When was the WWI armistice signed?
items.why: Signed in a railway carriage at Compiègne at about 5am, it took effect at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month.

items.q: Portugal's famous custard tart?
items.why: Monks at Lisbon's Jerónimos Monastery are credited with the recipe, using yolks left over from starching clothes with egg whites.

items.q: The 1919 treaty that punished Germany?
items.why: It blamed Germany for the war and imposed heavy reparations, a resentment Hitler later exploited.

items.q: Portugal's melancholy folk music?
items.why: Fado expresses 'saudade', a longing for something lost. UNESCO recognised it in 2011.

items.q: Roughly how many British casualties on the first day of the Somme?
items.why: About 19,000 British soldiers were killed on 1 July 1916, the bloodiest day in British military history.

items.q: The Portuguese explorer who reached India by sea in 1498?
items.why: Da Gama sailed around Africa to Calicut in 1498, opening Portugal's sea route for the spice trade.

items.q: The style of fighting that defined the Western Front?
items.why: Machine guns and artillery made advances suicidal, so armies dug in along lines from the Channel to Switzerland.

items.q: The disaster that flattened Lisbon in 1755?
items.why: On All Saints' Day 1755 a massive quake, then a tsunami and fires killed tens of thousands and levelled the city.

items.q: WWII years?
items.why: The deadliest conflict in history killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people.

items.q: Portugal's alliance with England, the world's oldest still in force, dates from…?
items.why: The Treaty of Windsor in 1386, building on an earlier 1373 treaty. It was invoked as recently as the Falklands War.

items.q: What started WWII in Europe on 1 September 1939?
items.why: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on 3 September.

items.q: The 1974 bloodless coup that ended Portugal's dictatorship?
items.why: On 25 April 1974 soldiers ended the dictatorship almost without bloodshed. People put carnations in their rifles.

items.q: The main Axis powers?
items.why: They formalised their alliance in the 1940 Tripartite Pact.

items.q: The fortified wine from the Douro Valley?
items.why: Adding brandy stops fermentation, keeping the wine sweet and strong. British merchants made it famous.

items.q: The 'Big Three' Allied leaders?
items.why: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met at Tehran and Yalta to plan the war and the post-war world.

items.q: Capital of Albania?
items.why: In the 2000s the mayor had Tirana's grey communist blocks painted in bright colours.

items.q: The 1939 pact in which Hitler and Stalin agreed not to fight, and split Poland?
items.why: Signed in August 1939, it freed Hitler to invade Poland without fighting the USSR, until he invaded in 1941.

items.q: Albania's currency?
items.why: The lek is named after Alexander the Great, 'Leka' in Albanian.

items.q: When did the USSR join the Allies' fight?
items.why: In June 1941, when Germany broke their pact and invaded. In 1939 the USSR had split Poland with Germany.

items.q: Albania's popular beers?
items.why: Nikšićko is Montenegrin, Ožujsko Croatian and Mythos Greek.

items.q: What brought the USA into WWII?
items.a: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941
items.why: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. Four days later Germany declared war on the US.

items.q: Albania's communist dictator from 1944 to 1985?
items.why: Hoxha cut Albania off from almost the entire world, breaking with Yugoslavia, the USSR and finally China.

items.q: The 1940 air battle over England?
items.why: The RAF beat back the Luftwaffe. Churchill said never had so much been owed by so many to so few.

items.q: What was banned for ordinary Albanians under communism?
items.why: Under Hoxha, private cars were banned, so roads were nearly empty apart from official vehicles.

items.q: The 1940 evacuation of 338,000 Allied troops from France?
items.why: Hundreds of civilian 'little ships' helped carry soldiers off the beaches in 1940.

items.q: Private car ownership became legal in Albania around…?
items.why: After communism fell, cars flooded in. Second-hand Mercedes quickly became the car of choice.

items.q: The brutal battle in Russia widely seen as the turning point of the war in Europe?
items.why: From 1942 to early 1943 the Soviets encircled and destroyed the German 6th Army at Stalingrad. Germany never recovered the initiative.

items.q: Roughly how many bunkers did Hoxha build?
items.why: That's roughly one bunker for every 17 people at the time. Many are now cafés, studios or storage.

items.q: D-Day, the Normandy landings, happened on…?
items.why: About 156,000 Allied troops landed on five Normandy beaches on the first day.

items.q: Why did Hoxha build so many bunkers?
items.why: Paranoid about attack from both East and West, his regime built around 170,000 concrete bunkers across Albania.

items.q: D-Day's code name?
items.why: Overlord was the whole invasion. Neptune was the name of the naval landing phase.

items.q: Which famous nun was ethnically Albanian?
items.why: Born in Skopje in 1910, she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her work in Calcutta.

items.q: Germany's 1941 invasion of the USSR?
items.why: Launched on 22 June 1941, it was the largest land invasion in history.

items.q: Albania's national hero who fought the Ottomans?
items.why: Skanderbeg held off the Ottomans for about 25 years in the 1400s.

items.q: VE Day, victory in Europe?
items.why: Because Germany signed late in the evening, Russia marks Victory Day on 9 May.

items.q: What's on Albania's red flag?
items.why: The eagle comes from Skanderbeg's seal. Albanians call their country Shqipëria, roughly 'land of eagles'.

items.q: Australia's 1942 jungle campaign against Japan in Papua?
items.why: Australian troops fought along about 96 km of jungle track over the Owen Stanley Range in 1942.

items.q: Albania's turquoise beach village on the Riviera?
items.why: Small islands sit just offshore in turquoise water, across the strait from Corfu.

items.q: Japan formally surrendered aboard USS Missouri on…?
items.why: The ceremony in Tokyo Bay formally ended the war, weeks after Japan announced its surrender.

items.q: Albania's ancient Greek and Roman ruins near Ksamil?
items.why: Butrint layers Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Venetian ruins in a lagoon-side forest. It's UNESCO-listed.

items.q: Australian troops famously held which Libyan port in 1941, earning the name 'Rats of'…?
items.why: German propaganda mocked them as rats in holes, and they adopted the 'Rats of Tobruk' name with pride.

items.q: A common Albanian head gesture surprise?
items.why: Many Albanians shake the head for yes and nod for no, the reverse of most of Europe.

items.q: Which neutral country stayed out of WWII despite being surrounded by Axis powers?
items.why: Swiss armed neutrality and mountain defences helped keep it out of the war.

items.q: Albania's flaky pastry snack?
items.why: Filo pastry filled with cheese, spinach or meat, eaten at any time of day.

items.q: Capital of Montenegro?
items.why: Podgorica was called Titograd from 1946 to 1992, after Yugoslavia's leader Tito.

items.q: Montenegro's old royal capital?
items.why: Cetinje was the royal capital until 1918. Former embassies still line its streets.

items.q: What currency does Montenegro use, despite not being in the EU?
items.why: Montenegro adopted the Deutsche Mark in 1999, then switched to the euro, without joining the EU.

items.q: What does 'Montenegro' mean?
items.why: Venetians named it after the dark forests of Mount Lovćen. In Montenegrin it's Crna Gora.

items.q: Montenegro became independent from Serbia in…?
items.why: A 2006 referendum passed with about 55.5%, just over the 55% threshold the EU had set.

items.q: Montenegro's fjord-like bay with a walled old town?
items.why: The bay is really a drowned river canyon. Kotor's old town is UNESCO-listed.

items.q: Montenegro's most common beer?
items.why: Nikšićko has been brewed in the town of Nikšić since 1896.

items.q: Capital of Croatia?
items.why: Zagreb's upper town has a church with a colourful tiled roof showing the city and national coats of arms.

items.q: Croatia's currency since 2023?
items.why: In 2023 Croatia switched from the kuna to the euro and joined the Schengen zone on the same day.

items.q: Croatia's popular beers?
items.why: Ožujsko comes from Zagreb and Karlovačko from Karlovac.

items.q: Dubrovnik doubled as which city in Game of Thrones?
items.why: Dubrovnik's walls and Old Town played King's Landing, and tourism boomed.

items.q: Split's old town is built inside which Roman emperor's palace?
items.why: Diocletian retired to his seaside palace around AD 305. People later built a whole town inside its walls.

items.q: Croatia's famous national park of terraced lakes and waterfalls?
items.why: Sixteen terraced lakes are joined by waterfalls, their colours shifting with minerals and light.

items.q: Which accessory is said to come from Croatian soldiers?
items.why: Croatian mercenaries in 17th-century France wore knotted scarves, and the French called them 'cravates'.

items.q: Croatia reached which men's World Cup final?
items.why: They lost the 2018 final to France 4 to 2, a huge achievement for a country of about 4 million.

items.q: Which spotted dog breed is named after a Croatian region?
items.why: Named after Dalmatia, Croatia's Adriatic coast. They once ran alongside horse-drawn carriages.

items.q: Capital of Japan?
items.why: Edo was renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital', in 1868 when the emperor moved there.

items.q: Japan's capital for over 1,000 years before Tokyo?
items.why: Kyoto was the imperial capital from 794 to 1868 and was spared from the atomic bombing for its cultural treasures.

items.q: Height of Mount Fuji?
items.why: Fuji is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707. Climbing season runs only July to early September.

items.q: Japan's bullet train first ran in…?
items.why: The Shinkansen opened just before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and has an extraordinary safety record.

items.q: Japan's currency?
items.why: 'Yen' means 'round', as in a round coin. Its symbol is ¥.

items.q: Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August 1945. Nagasaki on…?
items.why: Nagasaki became the target on 9 August after clouds hid the primary target, Kokura.

items.q: Japan's big beer brands?
items.why: Also Sapporo and Suntory. Tsingtao is Chinese, Hite Korean and Singha Thai.

items.q: Japan's native religion of kami spirits?
items.why: Most Japanese people mix Shinto and Buddhist practices rather than choosing one.

items.q: Japan's imperial house is famous as…?
items.why: Tradition traces the line back to 660 BC. It is the oldest continuing hereditary monarchy in the world.

items.q: Roughly how many islands make up Japan?
items.why: A 2023 recount using digital maps found 14,125 islands, double the old figure. Four main islands hold most people.

items.q: The Japanese practice of 'forest bathing'?
items.why: The term was coined in 1982. Studies link time among trees to lower stress hormones.
